utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-87-A, the Prosecutor versus Nikola Sainovic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, Vladimir Lazarevic, and Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As indicated, if any parties are unable to follow the proceedings at any stage, I ask them to bring this to my attention immediately. For the sake of the record, may I -- may we have the appearances of the parties. First, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Peter Kremer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. Joining me this morning is my colleague Michelle Jarvis. She's assisted by Najwa Nabti, Priya Gopalan. Also assisting this morning and making submissions will be Mr. Nema Milaninia, and again we're joined by our colleague Colin Nawrot, our Case Manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Tomo Fila. Next to me is Vladimir Petrovic and we still represent the accused Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. John Ackerman along with Aleksandar Aleksic for General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For Mr. Vladimir Lazarevic, Mihajlo Bakrac, Djuro Cepic, and our intern Milan Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Dan Ivetic for Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning we'll hear the appeals of the Prosecution. Now, counsel for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. To provide you with a road map of our submissions today, my colleagues Ms. Jarvis and Mr. Milaninia and I have divided the Prosecution's case and limited ourselves to four of the six grounds in our Notice of Appeal and appeal brief. Ms. Jarvis will make submissions on grounds 3 and 4 pertaining to the Chamber's errors concerning the crimes of persecution involving sexual violence. Mr. Milaninia will then briefly make submissions on ground 2 regarding the Chamber's erroneous acquittal of General Lazarevic for aiding and abetting murders involving the VJ. And I will conclude by addressing the Chamber's sentencing errors. We will not make submissions on grounds 1 and 5. These grounds concern technical legal errors and are fully briefed in our written submissions. If questions arise from the Bench or during the course of submissions by Defence, we will deal with those in reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Jarvis.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. As Mr. Kremer has just mentioned, I'm going to be addressing you this morning in relation to the Prosecution's third and fourth grounds of appeal which relate to the treatment of sexual assaults as persecution. Ground 3 concerns the Trial Chamber's error in failing to find that sexual assaults were foreseeable to Sainovic and to Lukic under the JCE III standard. And ground 4 concerns the Trial Chamber's error in failing to find that the sexual assaults that occurred in Pristina were committed with the discriminatory intent required for persecution, and this error affects the convictions of Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic. Presently, Your Honours, the outcome of this case stands for the proposition that in the midst of a violent ethnically driven expulsion campaign where women and girls are expelled from their homes in a highly volatile and terrifying atmosphere, where they are left at the mercy of tens of thousands of armed military and police forces, and where there are no effective protective mechanisms in place, acts of sexual violence are not foreseeable. A further implication of the trial judgement currently is that unless a perpetrator makes an expressly discriminatory statement at the time of inflicting an act of sexual assault, discriminatory intent for persecution cannot be found. Your Honours, it is important that we look carefully at both of those conclusions. For almost two decades, the ICTY has fairly and appropriately corrected many of the historical misconceptions surrounding wartime sexual violence crimes. At this stage, the ICTY should not leave as part of its legacy the perception that these crimes are subjected to higher standards of foreseeability or more onerous standards of proof concerning discriminatory intent. It is equally important to establish accountability for these crimes, Your Honour. You must focus on whether under the applicable criminal standards the Trial Chamber erred in assessing the culpability of the accused in this case. In our submission, it did. My argument today will proceed as follows. First I will address Your Honours in relation to ground 3 concerning the foreseeability of the sexual assault persecution. I'll explain that the Trial Chamber erred in applying too high a risk threshold for JCE III. I'll then discuss why, in correcting that legal error, Your Honours should be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that persecution based on sexual assaults was foreseeable to the JCE members, including Sainovic and Lukic. Second, I'll address Your Honours in relation to ground 4 concerning discriminatory intent for persecution. I'll explain why, given all of the prevailing contextual factors surrounding the rapes, the only reasonable conclusion is that they were committed with discriminatory intent. I'll also explain why, having corrected the Trial Chamber's errors, Your Honours should confirm that the Pristina rapes constitute persecution and enter convictions under JCE III for Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic. Turning first to the Prosecution's third ground of appeal. Before I proceed, Your Honours, I do want to make it clear that the Prosecution does not maintain the argument initially put forward in its appeal brief that Sainovic and Lukic had actual notice that sexual assaults were happening prior to the commencement of the 1999 campaign. As we mentioned in our reply brief, we accept that the evidence does not unequivocally support that proposition. However, in our submission, this in no way affects the viability of our ground of appeal. For the reasons that I'll explain, proof of prior notice that the same crimes have previously happened is not required to prove foreseeability. Your Honours, it is clear that the Trial Chamber has committed a legal error by applying too high a risk threshold for JCE III. The Trial Chamber required proof that the JCE members could foresee that sexual assaults would happen, relying on a decision that the Appeals Chamber has since confirmed is not good law. It should instead have considered whether the JCE members could foresee that sexual assault persecutions might happen, which equates with a possibility risk threshold. And the Appeals Chamber has, of course, settled this issue in its interlocutory appeal decision in the Karadzic case dated 25 June 2009. The Karadzic Appeals Chamber specifically noted that JCE III mens rea is satisfied if there is a possibility of the crime. Certainly we acknowledge that the Appeals Chamber cautioned that the standard will not be satisfied by implausibly remote scenarios and that there must be a sufficiently substantial possibility of the crime happening to make it foreseeable to the particular accused person in question. But nevertheless, the Appeals Chamber confirmed that requiring proof of a probability of the crime is setting the bar too high. That's at paragraph 18 of the Karadzic decision. So there has been a clear legal error. Your Honours must now apply the correct legal standard -the possibility risk threshold - to the Trial Chamber's factual findings and the evidence on the record and decide whether you are satisfied that the possibility of sexual assault persecutions was foreseeable to Sainovic and Lukic in the course of implementing the common criminal purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, would you be kind enough to point out a specific paragraph of the judgement where you claim that the Trial Chamber made an error in applying the wrong standards.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I could give a brief answer initially by saying that we have, of course, identified the relevant paragraphs in our Notice of Appeal but I can also take you through them as well. If you allow me just one moment to find the relevant passages. Your Honours, in particular in Volume I of the Trial Judgement at paragraphs 96 and 111, when we see, for example, in paragraph 190 -- sorry, in paragraph 96, if you move towards the end of that paragraph on page 40, the Trial Chamber has indicated it was looking to see whether it was reasonably foreseeable to him that the crime or underlying offence would be perpetrated by one or more of the persons used by him, being a member of the JCE. And this same language is then repeated in paragraph 111 of Volume I. And again I take you to the end of the paragraph on page 46, and we see again reference to it being reasonably foreseeable on the basis of the information available to the accused that the crime or underlying offence would be committed. The language of "would" is clearly incorrect and that has been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. The relevant language should be "might be committed," which does equate to a lower risk threshold that is equivalent to a possibility threshold. We see, Your Honours, similar language being repeated in Volume III of the Trial Judgement when the Chamber came to make its findings in relation to JCE III, and in particular, in relation to the accused Lukic, the Trial Chamber uses the term whether the sexual assaults were "likely," which again we say is indicative of the wrong legal threshold. Your Honours, more generally, the Trial Chamber in formulating this language was relying on the Brdjanin interlocutory appeal decision which did adopt the higher probability standard, and this was the very decision that in the Karadzic case the Appeals Chamber confirmed was too high a standard and had been implicitly overturned by other authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, foreseeability for the purposes of JCE III must be assessed with reference to the overall context in which the crimes were committed and particularly in light of the nature of the common criminal purpose. While evidence that the accused knew the same types of crimes had previously happened might be one relevant contextual factor, it is certainly not an essential ingredient in proving foreseeability. There are many other contextual factors that we say are relevant, and we ask Your Honours to make this point clear when rendering your judgement in this case. To illustrate the point, Your Honours, let's take for a moment the classical JCE III scenario where an accused person is held responsible for murder as a participant in a JCE to commit an armed bank robbery, even though it was never intended that anyone would actually be shot in the course of the robbery. The assessment that murder is a foreseeable consequence of the JCE III of the armed robbery doesn't depend on evidence that the participants in the JCE knew that bank staff had recently been shot in the course of other armed robberies. It's a matter of common sense. If someone charges into a bank with a loaded weapon to steal valuables, it's foreseeable that someone might be killed. Compare this to the JCE in this case. Instead of one loaded gun, tens of thousands of armed men unleashed into villages, including going door-to-door using violence and terror to forcibly displace upwards of 700.000 people, including, of course, women and girls. Your Honours must ask yourselves what crimes are foreseeable in this context? This approach has been previously adopted by many Trial Chambers and endorsed by the Appeals Chamber. And the Krstic case, Your Honours, is a very clear example. In finding that sexual violence was a foreseeable consequence of the humanitarian crisis in Potocari, the Trial Chamber did not require evidence that General Krstic knew his troops had previously been raped [sic]. Instead, the Trial Chamber drew common sense inferences based on an ordinary understanding of human behaviour, given the prevailing contextual factors and given the nature of the common criminal plan which was to displace women and children and elderly from the area. So the Trial Chamber emphasised the lack of shelter, the density of the crowds, the vulnerable condition of the refugees, the presence of many regular and irregular military and paramilitary units in the area and the sheer lack of protection available for the refugees. General Krstic knew enough about these prevailing contextual factors to make it foreseeable to him that women might be raped in this context. I refer you to paragraph 616 to 617 of the Krstic trial judgement and the Appeals Chamber endorsed this analysis at paragraph 149 of its appeal judgement. The Kvocka case is another clear example of a contextual analysis. In finding that sexual violence was foreseeable in the context of the Omarska prison camp in Prijedor municipality, the Trial Chamber did not require evidence the accused knew women had been previously raped in the camp. Instead, again, the Trial Chamber drew common sense inferences based on an ordinary understanding of human behaviour given the prevailing contextual factors and given the criminal plan to persecute and subjugate the non-Serb detainees. The Trial Chamber concluded, and the text will appear on your screens, Your Honours: "Indeed it would be -- indeed, it would be unrealistic and contrary to all rational logic to expect that none of the women held in Omarska, placed in circumstances rendering them especially vulnerable, would be subjected to rape or other forms of sexual violence." That's at paragraph 327 of the Kvocka trial judgement. To the Krstic and Kvocka precedents we can now also add the Tolimir trial judgement rendered in December last year. Although the Tolimir case didn't deal expressly with sexual violence crimes, the overall approach to foreseeability under JCE III is instructive and consistent with the Krstic and Kvocka precedents. It's at paragraphs 1136 and 1140 of the Tolimir trial judgement. Your Honours, if you carry out a similar contextual analysis in this case, the only reasonable conclusion is that Sainovic and Lukic could foresee that sexual assault persecution might happen in the context of this joint criminal enterprise. This conclusion is reinforced by Judge Chowhan's analysis in his dissenting opinion in this case. In finding sexual assaults were foreseeable, Judge Chowhan relied on factors including the involvement of able-bodied Serb forces, a common plan in which expulsion was achieved using violence, and the removal of women from their homes. Judge Chowhan's reference to prudence and common sense shows that he was applying everyday understandings of human dynamics in the context of the common purpose in question. That, we say, was the right approach and the one that Your Honours should adopt in this case. Your Honours, the regrettable truth is that we still live in a world where sexual violence against women is commonplace. In the chaos and aggression of armed conflict, when normal social structures have broken down, the risk is higher again. And certainly, Your Honours, in the midst of a violent ethnic cleansing campaign like the one in this case, to say that violations of physical integrity such as sexual assault was not even a foreseeable possibility would be to close our eyes to human experience. I want to highlight three main indicators in this case that we say made the possibility of sexual assault foreseeable to Sainovic and Lukic. They are, first of all, the use of violence and terror as an integral part of the common criminal purpose. Second, the prevailing climate of intense ethnic animosity. And third, the fact that women and girls were left in an utterly vulnerable position without normal protective measures functioning. ICTY case law confirms the relevance of each of these predictive factors in predicting sexual violence or other violent crimes. For example, I refer Your Honours to the Krstic trial judgement, paragraph 616, and the appeal judgement, paragraph 149; the Kvocka trial judgement, paragraph 327; the Popovic trial judgement, paragraph 1088; and the Tolimir trial judgement, paragraph 1136. So turning to the first indicator, the use of violence and terror by armed Serb forces as an integral part of the expulsion campaign. Your Honours, it would be unrealistic to expect that upwards of 700.000 people, Kosovo Albanians, would calmly agree to leave their homes never to return on the basis of a polite request. It's obvious that in order to permanently uproot so many people, the armed Serb forces had to use violence, including door-to-door expulsions, to terrify the targeted population into fleeing. And the Trial Chamber found exactly that. The judgement is replete with references underscoring the use of violence and terror as a part of the expulsion campaign. For example, and Your Honours will see the language on your screens, the Trial Chamber was satisfied that there was: "A broad campaign of violence directed against the Kosovo Albanian civilian population during the course of the NATO air strikes ..." That's Volume II, paragraph 1156. The Trial Chamber also found: "... consistent eyewitness accounts of the systematic terrorisation of Kosovo Albanian civilians by forces of the FRY and Serbia, their removal from their homes, and the looting and deliberate destruction of property, satisfies the Chamber that there was campaign of violence directed against the Kosovo Albanian civilian population, during which there were incidents of killing, sexual assault, and the intentional destruction of mosques." That's Volume II, paragraph 1178, and I refer to you a similar finding at paragraph 1156. Most importantly, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was satisfied that the use of violence and terror was an essential component of the common criminal purpose and again you'll see the text appearing on your screens. The Trial Chamber formulated the common purpose this way, it said: "Through a widespread and systematic campaign of terror and violence, the Kosovo Albanian population was to be forcibly displaced both within and without Kosovo." That's Volume III, paragraph 95. It is important that we understand sexual assaults were violent crimes committed in the course of this violent attack, just like the violent expulsions, murders, beatings, and property damage. The gang-rape of Witness K20 in Beleg is a clear example. Serb forces arrived in Beleg with armoured vehicles and began mistreating the Kosovo Albanian population. Personal documents were confiscated, men were beaten and murdered, and women were strip-searched and subjected to sexual violence. That's paragraph -- Volume II paragraphs 54 to 55, 58 to 64. Armed Serb forces surrounded K20's home and ordered her and her family to leave. There were imprisoned in a stifling basement with around 300 other prisoners, many of whom were women. K20 was taken out with four other girls and violently gang-raped by four soldiers. At the same time, she could hear the screams of two other girls and she knew that they were being raped too. Afterwards she was in such severe pain that she could not sit and she lost consciousness. The next day, a policeman ordered K20 and the other detainees: "Go to Albania, you have asked for NATO." The villagers of Beleg fled Kosovo, like the hundreds of thousands of other Kosovo Albanians. K20 was among them. She had been evicted from her home, imprisoned in inhumane conditions, raped, and finally expelled from Kosovo, fulfilling the aims of the JCE. That's Volume II, paragraphs 58, 61, 65, 67, 1178; and Exhibit P2669 at pages 2, and 4 to 6. The experiences of the sexual assault witnesses in Qirez bear the same hallmarks. Men were killed at will, homes and property burned, and women were forced to flee from place to place and were sexual assaulted. That's Volume II, paragraphs 623 to 636. While the forms of physical violence inflicted on the Kosovo Albanian population took on different dimensions depending on whether they were men or women, they were all subjected to violence that made them flee. It is important to remember that the crime we're dealing with here is persecution based on violations of physical integrity. We should not lose sight of the fact that these sexual assaults, like all other acts of violence to the person, are about the use of physical force to injure and damage human beings. The Trial Chamber found that both Sainovic and Lukic knew that the displacement would be effected by violence and terror. In particular, the Trial Chamber found that this was one of the factors making property destruction foreseeable to them -- to each of them. That's Volume III, paragraphs 473 and 1136. Similarly, in finding that murder was foreseeable to Sainovic and Lukic, the Trial Chamber specifically referred to "the context in which the forcible displacement took place." That's Volume III, paragraphs 470 and 1134. This context obviously included the overwhelmingly violent and terrifying nature of the campaign. If the overarching use of violence and terror in carrying out the expulsion campaign is relevant in predicting violations of physical integrity like murder, then it is equally relevant in predicting violations of physical integrity like sexual assault. Similarly, if it's relevant in predicting property damage, it is certainly relevant in predicting physical damage to the female members of that same group. Human experience tells us that the violent acts committed against women very often take on different forms in the context of a campaign like the 1999 expulsion campaign in Kosovo. It is important that the law recognises and responds adequately to the experiences of everyone. A second indicator of sexual assault persecution in this case is the strong ethnic animosity that permeated the displacement campaign in Kosovo in 1999. This led to a volatile and highly charged situation. In indeed in this case the Trial Chamber relied on ethnic animosity and division as a factor in finding that both Sainovic and Lukic could foresee murder and the destruction of religious property. That is Volume III, paragraphs 470, 473, 1134, and 1136. Again, Your Honours, if it's a relevant factor in predicting murder and the destruction of property belonging to the targeted ethnic group, then it is certainly a relevant factor in predicting violent acts of persecution such as sexual assault on the women of that same ethnic group. A third evidentiary indicator of sexual assault persecution in this case is the fact that the Kosovo women and girls were left in an utterly vulnerable situation without normal protective measures functioning. They were forced from their homes and left at the mercy of the armed Serb forces who exercised total power over them. Sainovic and Lukic were well aware of the vulnerable position of the women and girls. First, the whole point of the criminal plan they endorsed was to force the Kosovo Albanian population, including the women and girls, from the safety and security of their homes. Second, from their experience in 1998, both accused knew that this criminal plan would likely result in a humanitarian crisis -- catastrophe and a refugee crisis. That's Volume III, paragraphs 442 and 1079. This was confirmed by what they saw in Pristina during the JCE's implementation. The Trial Chamber found that during the NATO campaign Sainovic was again a very well-informed politician when it came to the events in Kosovo, and that he had a detailed knowledge of events on the ground in Kosovo in both 1998 and 1999. That's Volume III, paragraphs 464 and 470. Sainovic was in Pristina during periods when massive expulsions were taking place there, involving door-to-door searches and terrifying the Kosovo Albanian population with threats, beatings and gunfire as they moved in confined columns. That's set out in our appeal brief at paragraph 79. Similarly, the Trial Chamber found Lukic had a detailed knowledge of events on the ground in 1998 and 1999. Volume III, paragraph 1134. Lukic was based at the MUP staff headquarters in Pristina and he knew ill-treatment and forcible displacements were occurring. That's Volume III, paragraph 1124. In addition to these three indicators I've mentioned so far, which are of themselves a sufficient basis to find the possibility of sexual assault was foreseeable, we also rely on the additional contextual factors set out in our appeal brief. In particular, in deploying the VJ and MUP forces in 1999 to expel the Kosovo Albanian population, Sainovic and Lukic knew that these same forces had in fact committed violent crimes including violations of physical integrity during the 1998 campaign. For example, I refer you to paragraph 70 of our appeal brief. Not only that, but the JCE members, including Sainovic and Lukic, used these same forces to carry out a vastly more extensive expulsion campaign without putting in place any meaningful safeguards. In this respect, I refer Your Honours to the approach taken by the ICTR in the Karemera trial judgement at paragraphs 1476 to 1477, finding that in the course of an extermination campaign to destroy a group, it is foreseeable that soldiers and militias who participate in the destruction will resort to rapes unless restricted by their superiors. Your Honours, if we were to conclude that sexual assault persecutions were not foreseeable in this case as a possible consequence, what then are we really saying about the nature of sexual assaults? Are we concerned that they were purely coincidental opportunistic assaults which weren't connected to the broader campaign? We know this is not the case, because the Trial Chamber expressly found that they were part of the widespread and systematic attack on the Kosovo Albanian population and therefore constituted crimes against humanity. That's Volume 2, paragraphs 1184, 1188, 1220, and 1224. By definition then, they were not a limited number of randomly selected individuals nor were they isolated acts. Are we concerned, Your Honours, that the number of sexual assaults in evidence in this case was not higher? First of all, we should be careful about the conclusion that the numbers were low. Although the Prosecution only charged the accused with 11 incidents and their responsibility is limited to those, that doesn't mean they were the only incidents documented on the record. There is evidence of around 50 additional sexual assaults. And I refer Your Honours to Volume 2, paragraphs 63, 629 to 636, 880; and Exhibit P2596. The Trial Chamber also referred to additional reports of rape and sexual violence committed during the 1999 campaign in official documents and meetings. I refer you to Volume III, paragraphs 552, 572, 576, 578, 585, 726, 737, 749, 785, and 1135. But more fundamentally, Your Honours, why should it matter even if only a small number of sexual assaults were in evidence? The question is whether a crime that is predictable based on the nature of the common purpose occurred, not whether it occurred in large numbers. Your Honours should instead focus on whether the violations of physical integrity stemming from the sexual assaults fits in with the overall pattern of violations of physical integrity in the violent campaign. We say they did, and as I've mentioned, the Trial Chamber's findings on the contextual elements of crimes against humanity very strongly support that conclusion. If we say that the sexual assault persecutions were not foreseeable, does this mean that we either do not regard them as violent acts or that we regard them as somehow qualitatively different from other violent acts? Neither of these propositions can be accepted either. Given the facts surrounding each of the incidents in this case, it's clear that the sexual assaults were about violence and control. Nor were these acts qualitatively different just because of their sexual component. The ICTY's previous case law has resoundingly rejected Defence arguments that seek to put sexual violence in a different category from other violent acts on the basis that one of the underlying motives might have been a desire for sexual gratification. And I refer Your Honours to the Kunarac appeal judgement, paragraphs 153 and 155. This case presents an opportunity for Your Honours to reinforce this point and it's an important one. Not only was the possibility of sexual assault persecution foreseeable to Sainovic and Lukic, but they willingly took the risk that it would happen by joining and continuing to participate in the criminal enterprise. Moreover, they took no meaningful steps to prevent the crimes from happening. And I refer Your Honours generally to the Trial Chamber's findings Volume III, paragraphs 458, 477 -- sorry, 458 to 477, and 1114 to 1140. Your Honours, the contextual analysis that we're advancing here does not result in an overly broad or unfair approach to responsibility. In this case we're not speaking about the general risk of sexual assault happening during conflict. We're speaking about the considerably heightened risk of it happening in the midst of a violent expulsion campaign to terrify a population into leaving. Your Honours, this brings me to the fourth ground of appeal concerning the classification as persecution of three rape incidents in Pristina in April and May 1999. The Trial Chamber accepted that the three rape incidents were proved but stated that the Prosecution had "failed to bring any evidence" from which it could infer that these rapes were carried out with the discriminatory intent required for persecution. That's Volume II, paragraph 1245. It is clear, again, that the Trial Chamber committed an error in saying that there was no relevant evidence. The Chamber failed to consider any of the general or specific contextual factors surrounding the rapes which are highly relevant to assessing discriminatory intent. In addition, in the case of Witness K31, the Trial Chamber failed to consider direct evidence of discriminatory intent in the form of a derogatory statement about Albanians made by one rapist. This was an error of law or alternatively an error of fact. You could consider it an error of law because the Trial Chamber improperly limited the scope of the evidence it considered relevant. Effectively it required evidence of a directly discriminatory statement in order to find persecution. Alternatively, Your Honours could approach it as an error of fact. Either way, the only reasonable conclusion is that the Pristina rapes were carried out with the discriminatory intent required for persecution. This is not the first time that the Appeals Chamber has been confronted with an issue similar to the one before Your Honours today. It also came up in the Krnojelac case. There too the Trial Chamber had failed to analyse the contextual surrounding circumstances of the crimes to infer discriminatory intent and the Appeals Chamber overturned the Trial Chamber's erroneous conclusions and substituted persecution convictions. For example, the Krnojelac appeal judgement at paragraphs 184 to 188. In doing so, the Appeals Chamber confirmed that the fact that something happens in the course of a broader discriminatory attack, doesn't, of course, mean that you can automatically infer it was also committed with discriminatory intent. But the Appeals Chamber also confirmed that if the circumstances surrounding the commission of the specific acts in question are consistent with that broader discriminatory context, then of course you can and should infer discrimination based on the whole package of relevant factors. Here, Your Honours, all the circumstances surrounding the rape incidents in Pristina confirm that they were an integral part of the discriminatory attack. We've set out the relevant factors in some detail in our appeal brief at paragraphs 87 to 100, and I won't go over them in detail here but I will highlight some of the key factors. It is important that we clearly understand the context in which these rapes happened. Everything that happened to the three Kosovo Albanian women - K31, K14, and K62 - was connected to their ethnicity. K31 saw villagers murdered around her during the attack on Pristina. Serb forces then captured her and her injured brother. Her hands were tied, she was threatened with death, and four soldiers tried to extract information from her about her uncle and so-called alleged terrorists. She was beaten, abused and sexual assaulted as the soldiers took her to the Pristina hospital. At the hospital, she was imprisoned in a basement with up to 15 other young Kosovo Albanian women who had apparently been brought there to be raped. She was drugged and brutally raped several times by three different soldiers. One of them cursed Albanians immediately after he raped her. The experiences of K14 and K62, the other Pristina witnesses, bear similar hallmarks. All three were Kosovo Albanian women targeted by Serb forces for expulsion, imprisonment and rape because they were Kosovo Albanian women. And the strategy was successful. As K14 explained, after being violently raped by Serb forces at the notorious Hotel Bozhur, she and her family fled. That's in the transcript at page 10990. Your Honours, nothing about the prevailing context shows that these rapes were somehow separate or isolated acts disconnected from the broader discriminatory attack. To paraphrase the Kvocka Trial Chamber at paragraph 195, when all the victims of this attack were Kosovo Albanian civilians and when all of the abusers were members of the Serb forces sent in to expel them from their homes using violence and terror, it is disingenuous to contend that ethnicity did not define the group targeted for attack, including the female members of the group. Once again, Your Honours, we have to think about what we're really saying here if we conclude that these rapes were not committed with discriminatory intent. Can we really accept that the Serb forces had a persecutory switch that was somehow turned off when these rapes occurred but was activated at all other times? If the Serb forces attacking and cleansing Pristina were acting with discriminatory intent when they murdered Kosovo Albanians and damaged Kosovo Albanian property, how could they suddenly not be acting with discriminatory intent when they raped and otherwise abused these three Kosovo Albanian women as part of the same course of conduct? Even if there are concerns that the perpetrators may have been motivated by the desire for sexual gratification, this would not preclude a finding of discriminatory intent. Similar arguments have been dismissed by the Appeals Chamber previously. And I refer to the Kunarac appeal judgement, paragraphs 153 and 155, finding that if a rape perpetrator's motivation is sexual, this does not preclude a finding that the rape was carried out with one of the prohibited purposes for torture. We say a similar analysis applies here in the context of persecution. Further, as confirmed by the Krnojelac trial judgement, paragraph 435, discriminatory intent for persecution need not be the primary intent with respect to the act, although it must be a significant one. I also refer Your Honours to the Kunarac appeal judgement once again, paragraph 153 and 155, for similar reasoning in the context of the crime of torture. The relief we've requested in relation to ground 4 is that Pavkovic, Sainovic, and Lukic should be convicted of the Pristina sexual assaults as a crime against humanity by way of persecution pursuant to JCE III. On correcting the Trial Chamber's error in its discriminatory intent analysis, all of the elements of persecution as a crime against humanity will be met. The Trial Chamber made a general finding that the crimes in Pristina were part of the widespread and systematic attack on the Kosovo Albanian population and that the physical perpetrators knew or took that risk. That's Volume II, paragraphs 889, 1240 to 1241. With respect to the responsibility of the JCE members for the Pristina rapes, the Trial Chamber made findings that the crimes were committed by the VJ and/or MUP personnel. Volume II, paragraph 889. The Trial Chamber also found that all of the indicted crimes of the VJ and MUP are attributable to each of the JCE members. That's Volume III, paragraphs 468, 783, and 1132. When it comes to the foreseeability of the Pristina sexual assaults for the purposes of JCE III, I refer to the submissions that I've already made today in respect of Sainovic and Lukic as supplemented by our appeal brief. And regarding Pavkovic, on Tuesday, my colleague Mr. Schneider answered Your Honours' question as to why the Pristina rapes were foreseeable to him. In conclusion, we ask Your Honours to make it clear in your judgement that this Tribunal will not subject sexual violence crimes to higher standards of foreseeability or higher proof requirements for discriminatory intent than other violent crimes. We also ask you to make it clear, as you have consistently done before, that this Tribunal recognises and appropriately sanctions the many forms of violence the victims in this conflict experienced, men and women alike, violence inflicted because of their status as members of the targeted population. That concludes my submissions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, concerning the so-called opportunistic sexual assault, I would like you to compare with the case in ICTR, that is Rukundo case. Although where the contextual circumstances is genocide, the majority of the Appeals Chamber still did not convict the accused as rape.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're aware of the Rukundo precedent, and, Your Honours, I think it would be important to say that of course each case has to be taken on a case-by-case basis having regard to its own contextual factors. In the context of Rukundo, as I recall the decision, the Appeals Chamber was looking at one incident of rape or sexual assault, I think it indeed was, and it was unable to find by majority -- there were of course different opinions on the Bench in that case, but the majority was unable to find that it was sufficiently connected to the broader attack to find that it constituted an act of genocide as I recall. In this case, Your Honour, for all the reasons that I've given, it is entirely different. We are talking about a violent ethnic cleansing campaign involving thousands -- tens of thousands of armed forces going door-to-door to expel the population. In this situation, we say it really is at odds with everything we know about the way the world operates, the way conflict operates, the way violent expulsion campaigns operate, to find that sexual assault would not even be foreseeable as a possibility. Indeed, all of the other Trial Chambers' findings point in that same direction. They accepted that this wasn't some separate opportunistic isolated act. Otherwise, they would not have found that it formed part of the widespread and systematic attack. They accepted that the crimes, apart from the Pristina ones, which is subject to our ground 4, were committed with discriminatory intent. Again, something that shows these were part and parcel of the campaign. In those circumstances, Your Honours, we ask you, in correcting the Trial Chamber's legal error, to really ask yourselves whether you are satisfied that these acts were foreseeable and that they were committed with discriminatory intent. And for all the reasons that I've given, we say your answer should be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge T also has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Jarvis, this may be a recurring theme from yesterday, but yesterday I asked a question of your colleague Ms. Kravetz about the possible, if identifiable, specific exclusion by the Trial Chamber of the possibility that other factors during the armed conflict, apart from sexual assaults or murder or damage, and destruction of religious objects, for that matter, could have contributed to the displacement of at least some of the 700.000 Kosovo Albanians. And my question yesterday was initially answered by Ms. Kravetz, and then after the break, having done some homework, Mr. Wood supplemented her initial answer with reference to particular paragraphs of different volumes of judgements, thus implicitly and discreetly, and in very polite manner, inviting me to do some homework which I had to do even though at the expense of a glass of wine over supper. And I think that after this homework the question remains, because looking at the paragraphs to which Mr. Wood directed my attention, I discovered only one very specific, up to a single number, reference to the numbers of Kosovo Albanians who crossed the border from Kosovo into Albania and Macedonia, and that was referenced to reports that were sent by the MUP personnel on the ground through the MUP channels to Belgrade headquarters, and that number was 715.158 during the period from 24 March to 1 May. My further accomplishment while working on that home assignment proved that the Trial Chamber in paragraph 1175 of Volume II, which Mr. Wood directed my attention to, was mindful of the fact that people may have left their homes for different reasons and there were several reasons unrelated to the primary reason of crimes including sexual assault. So I guess my question remains, while the Trial Chamber Volume II is using the language of almost 700.000 Kosovo Albanians being displaced, your language was different and twice you referred to forcible displacement of, and I quote, "upwards of 700.000 humans." So I guess my question remains, that is whether you could direct me to the Trial Chamber where it beyond reasonable doubt, based on evidence other than reports of the MUP, made a conclusion that the displacement of almost or upwards of 700.000 could be attributed to the common plan of members of JCE. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that that's a question we could come back to you with perhaps after the break or during our reply as I would need to take some time to check the -- the judgement and the evidentiary records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Certainly, but not at the expense of your lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think it's quite enough that you had to take up time last night. We certainly won't interfere with lunch plans today. But given the history of this and given the answers that have already been given to you by my colleagues, Ms. Kravetz and Mr. Wood, I think it would make most sense and would be of most assistance to Your Honours if we could have a moment to consider our answer and get back to you with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me there's no questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, as Mr. Kremer has indicated earlier this morning, I intend to cover very briefly ground 2 of our appeal concerning the acquittal of General Lazarevic for aiding and abetting the murders in Korenica, Meja, and Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's legal error which caused it to acquit General Lazarevic of these crimes can be found at Volume III, paragraph 928 of the judgement where it specifically requires that General Lazarevic be aware that VJ and MUP forces were going to commit murders at the specific crime sites at issue. Your Honours, this Tribunal has rejected this type of precision for the mens rea of aiding and abetting. The mens rea for aiding and abetting only requires awareness of the likelihood that the crime will be committed and that one's acts and omissions will contribute to that crime. It does not require, Your Honours, awareness as to where, when, or even how that crime will be committed. This principle was enunciated in the Simic appeals judgement at paragraph 86, and was further explained in the Oric trial judgement at paragraph 288, which explicitly noted that the aider and abettor need not foresee "the place, time, and number of the precise crimes." Your Honours, I also refer you to paragraphs 37 and 38 of our appeals brief for additional legal support. When applying the correct standard in this case, the Trial Chamber made clear findings that General Lazarevic was aware that murders were likely to be committed by his VJ forces. Indeed, the Chamber admits at Volume III, paragraph 928, that General Lazarevic was aware of VJ members killing Kosovo Albanians in some instances. That knowledge, Your Honours, was established by the Chamber's findings that throughout 1998 and 1999 and before the killings at issue, General Lazarevic was constantly informed of VJ involvement in the murder of Kosovo Albanian civilians. Your Honours, we detailed those findings in full in our brief at paragraphs 49 to 47 [sic]. However, for your convenience, I'll quickly highlight a few of those. The Trial Chamber found that at the end of 1998, General Lazarevic knew of VJ involvement in the killings of Kosovo Albanian civilians. For instance, he was informed of UN Security Council Resolution 1199 which noted that excessive and indiscriminate force by the VJ had resulted in numerous civilian casualties. From the beginning of the 1999 campaign, VJ forces continued to target and kill Kosovo Albanian civilians. For example, Your Honours, by the end of March 1999, a few days into the campaign, General Lazarevic was informed of the killing of Kosovo Albanians in the village of Zegra. A week later, at the start of April 1999, General Lazarevic was aware of a press release stating that Serb forces were responsible for killing Kosovo Albanians in the villages of Pudojevo, Pec, and in the Orahovac municipality. A few days later, on April 3rd, 1999, General Lazarevic himself noted the receipt of numerous criminal reports including those for murder. And, Your Honours, a few weeks later, on April 26, 1999, the day before the massacres in Korenica and Meja, General Lazarevic was informed that his subordinates may have executed 20 Kosovo Albanian civilians in the village of Mali Alas just a week earlier. And approximately one month later, on May 24th, 1999, after the murders in Korenica and Meja, and a day before the murders in Dubrava, General Lazarevic himself issued a report discussing murders being committed throughout the Kosovo campaign at mixed MUP-VJ military check-points and warning about future crimes. Your Honours, General Lazarevic was also aware that a central component of the 1999 campaign was a use of force and violence against Kosovo Albanian civilians. You can find that at Volume III, paragraphs 855 and 924. The use of violence was particularly likely in the Reka Valley operation, during which the massacres in Korenica and Meja occurred, given that the operation was specifically undertaken to revenge the killing of five policemen on April 22nd, 1999. You can find that at Volume II, paragraphs 168 and 179. Your Honours, to conclude my remarks on the Chamber's findings regarding mens rea, I simply remind you that these are examples of a sample of the Chamber's findings concerning General Lazarevic's knowledge of the murders of Kosovo Albanian civilians by the VJ. For the Chamber's findings concerning actus reus, Your Honours, I refer you to our written submissions and also Volume III, paragraphs 923, 829 and 925, which discuss how, with this knowledge, General Lazarevic ordered the VJ to operate in Kosovo in 1999 and continued throughout May and June to participate in planning the joint operations. I wish to make one final note before I pass the podium to my colleague Mr. Kremer that with regards to the specific direction requirement established in the Perisic appeal judgement, I simply note and incorporate the detailed submissions made by my colleague Mr. Marcussen on Wednesday. To summarise Mr. Marcussen's points, there are four cogent reasons to depart from the Perisic appeals judgement. Further, to the extent specific direction is an element of aiding and abetting, it was established implicitly in this case, first, General Lazarevic was on the ground in Kosovo during the campaign in which the murders were committed. For this reason alone, his acts and omissions must be considered proximate to the crimes. Second, General Lazarevic must be considered a proximate aider and abettor as he was the commander of the forces involved in the murders. And lastly, as noted by Mr. Marcussen on Wednesday, he detailed the relationship between General Lazarevic acts and conduct and the crimes committed in Korenica, Meja, and Dubrava. Accordingly, Your Honours, the culpable link between General Lazarevic's acts and omissions and the murders were established in this case. Your Honours, due to the brevity of time and in order to enable Mr. Kremer to do a fuller submission on sentencing, that concludes my submissions on ground 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I will deal with ground 6, the Prosecution appeal from the sentences imposed by the Trial Chamber on the accused. Your Honours have heard that in a little over two months, beginning in late March 1999, the accused together, through their individual contributions, ruined the lives of over 700.000 Kosovo Albanians by forcing them from their homes and displacing them into Albania, Macedonia, and Montenegro. The sentences of 22 years' imprisonment for the JCE members Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic and 15 years for the aider and abettor Lazarevic were wholly inadequate and manifestly disproportionate to the gravity of the crimes and their role and degree of participation. It is our submission, as set out more fully in our brief, that the Appeals Chamber should set aside these sentences and substantially increase them for each of the four accused. One cannot sensibly talk about the Chamber's errors in sentencing without first discussing the crimes for which the accused were convicted. Throughout the week and even this morning, the Chamber has received but a glimpse of the scale and cruelty of the crimes committed against Kosovo Albanians in 1999, as well as the systematic and premeditated nature of those crimes. The Chamber has also received submissions regarding the role each accused played in orchestrating and executing these crimes. As the Chamber has already heard, on 24 March 1999 and under the cover of the NATO bombings, VJ and MUP forces launched a co-ordinated campaign of violence and terror throughout Kosovo intended to expel the Kosovo Albanian population. Almost every major town in Kosovo was attacked in the campaign's first three days. Over 600.000 Kosovo Albanians were expelled by the end of the campaign's second week. By the beginning of June 1999, the Chamber found that the forcible displacement and other crimes were committed by Serb forces in over 27 towns and villages throughout 13 representative municipalities. Today I will give you a brief picture of the scale and nature of these crimes and their impact on victims. I will not -- try not to repeat what has been said earlier this week or this morning, and I will start with Pristina, which exemplifies the crimes committed throughout the larger towns in Kosovo. The attacks in Pristina can be found in Volume II, paragraphs 801 to 890. On March 24th, 1999, and simultaneous to the beginning of the NATO attacks, the VJ and the MUP and other armed Serb forces began their attack on the large Kosovo population in Pristina. Months and weeks in advance of the attacks in Pristina, VJ and MUP forces laid the groundwork for the mass expulsion campaign through the secret arming and disarming process and by reinforcing MUP, VJ, and Serb military forces in and around Pristina despite the absence of significant KLA presence in the area. From the outset, Kosovo Albanians were subject to threats and acts of violence, including beatings, murder, the looting and burning of homes, the sexual abuse of women, and forced evictions. I refer you to Volume II, paragraph 885. VJ and MUP forces targeted and murdered prominent Kosovo Albanians as a clear message to other civilians of what was to come and to frighten them to flee. Volume II, paragraph 823. Expulsions were an almost daily occurrence from the 24th of March until at least 3 April 1999. And that's found in Volume II, paragraph 817 to 832. In some instances, armed VJ and MUP forces went from home to home forcibly evicting Albanians into the streets and threatening them to leave. Your Honours, the following slide is a quote from K63's written statement, Exhibit P2443. K63 was a Kosovo Albanian found credible and relied upon by the Trial Chamber. I refer you to paragraphs 805 and 839 of Volume II. He and his wife, K62, who you've heard about already, she was a victim of the Pristina rapes, resided in Pristina before being forcibly expelled. He said in the statement: "I saw police going to flats and ordering the Albanians out. They would say, 'Go to Albania, Kosovo is not your land.' I saw that once people left their flats with nothing more than a bag of food and clothing, that the police moved in and positioned themselves in those flats." Dr. Emin Kabashi, another Albanian resident in Pristina, noted that he received calls from Serbs telling him to leave for Albania or else he would be killed. Volume 2, paragraph 828. Once the Albanians were forced from their homes, VJ and MUP forces in Pristina put doors -- put signs on doors of vacated Albanian homes, stating: "This is a MUP apartment." Many of these homes were then occupied by the VJ and MUP themselves and used to house official organs of the FRY and Serbian government. Volume II, paragraphs 832 and 833. Daily, thousands of Kosovo Albanian Pristina residents were herded into the centre of town and formed into a convoy. As they left the town centre, carefully positioned policemen and soldiers pointed their weapons to direct them and the flow of the Kosovo Albanians. Volume II, paragraph 841, 848, 849, and 885. The convoys were directed down the main road past exit points with armed Serb forces to the town's train centre -- or train station. Volume II, paragraph 850. Kosovo Albanians who attempted to flee the convoy were mistreated or killed. Snipers were positioned in a nearby building. Volume II, paragraph 846. Thousands of Kosovo Albanians from the Pristina municipality gathered at the train station where they were forced onto trains or onto buses outside the station and taken to the Macedonian border. Volume II, paragraphs 852 to 864. Nazlie Bala, a Kosovo Albanian resident of Pristina, noted that the train that she was forced onto carried armed MUP and VJ personnel on the first and last cars. The train was so crowded, she said, that it was difficult to breathe. Volume II, paragraph 854. Dr. Kabashi was at the train station for three days and three nights before he was forced to board a goods train that took him to the Macedonian border. He saw five to 12 trains arriving at the station every day, leaving with people who were forced onto the train by the police. He noted that the Albanians were herded like cattle. Volume II, paragraph 856. The Chamber concluded that during the displacement campaign, the train schedules were purposefully modified so that a greater number of trains than usual would arrive at Pristina carrying more than the usual number of cars. These changes demonstrated a high level of co-ordination between not only the VJ and MUP forces carrying out the displacement campaign but also the railway agencies. That's at Volume II, paragraph 854. At stops during the train journey to the border, the Kosovo Albanians were subject to abuse and threats. The trains were surrounded by Serb forces. VJ and MUP forces shouted insults at the Kosovo Albanians, cursing at them and shouting, "Kosovo does not belong to you, Albanians. It belongs to Serbs. We're going to kill you, Albanians." Volume II, paragraph 859. When the trains reached the Macedonian border, the Kosovo Albanians were told to disembark, form a line and walk in the middle of the train tracks to avoid land mines. Their identity documents and passports were seized and destroyed. Finally, at gunpoint, the Kosovo Albanians were forced to cross the border into Macedonia. I refer you to paragraph -- Volume II, paragraphs 860 to 863, and 973. I highlight the written statement of Dr. Kabashi, Exhibit 2252, which was used in the trial judgement and this is before you now. And I think it poignantly sets out the result and the impact of the victims who were forced to leave Pristina and Kosovo. He said: "I did not want to leave Kosovo. We left because we were forced by the actions and words of the Serb police and army to leave. As a family, we were not organised to fight. I do not know who can stay in Kosovo when threatened by gun. The population was totally undefended. We were mainly the elderly, women, and children. If you had seen the sights at the train station in Bllaca, you would have thought that all of the children in the world had gathered there. The reality of the situation was displayed at the railway station and at Bllaca in that there was not a single person who was not in tears. This was not a road where these columns passed -- there was not a road where these columns passed where there were not dead people." The Trial Chamber found that the breadth of the crimes and the organised nature of the forced expulsions of Kosovo Albanians in the Pristina municipality were a result of significant planning and co-ordination at the highest levels of authority. Volume II, paragraph 888. And as my colleague Ms. Jarvis described this morning and you've heard earlier in submissions this week, Sainovic, Pavkovic, Lukic, and Lazarevic were all in Pristina town during these events. Let me now turn briefly to my second example, the VJ MUP attacks on Orahovac municipality. These illustrate how the campaign of terror and violence against the Kosovo Albanians was implemented in smaller towns and villages throughout Kosovo and that the attacks on Pristina and other large towns were not committed in isolation. On March 25th, 1999, the day after the attacks were launched in Pristina, VJ and MUP forces launched a wave of attacks in the Orahovac municipality, on the towns of Celina, Pirane, Bela Crkva and Mala Krusa, four towns located in the south-west region of Kosovo near the province's border with Albania. As has been discussed this week, these attacks were ordered by the Joint Command two days earlier, directing a joint action between the 549th Motorised Brigade and the MUP. That's Volume II, paragraph 296. On the morning of March 25th, VJ tanks together with MUP forces began shooting towards Bela Crkva as a warning to Albanian civilians to leave the village. Serb forces then entered the village and together with local police set Kosovo Albanian houses on fire using petrol and flame throwers. Upon hearing the shooting, Kosovo Albanian villagers began to flee to the Belaja stream to conceal themselves using the stream's high banks. And that's Volume II, paragraphs 341 and 343. MUP forces followed the villagers and began shooting at them with automatic weapons, killing at least 10 civilians, including women and children, while shouting, "Fuck your mother. Ask NATO for help now." Volume II, paragraphs 346 and 348. Of the remaining villagers, the women and children were separated from the men and ordered towards the direction of Albania. The men were ordered to strip to their underwear, robbed of their valuables, and had their passports, identity cards and driver's licenses destroyed. After being forced to climb down into the stream, at least 42 men were summarily executed. Volume II, paragraphs 350 to 354, 380 to 382, and 1161. Just south of Bela Crkva in the nearby town -- village of Celina, a similar matter of events unfolded simultaneously and these have been dealt with by Mr. Marcussen in his submissions. Simultaneous to the attacks in Celina and at Bela Crkva, VJ and MUP forces surrounded the village of Mala Krusa. VJ soldiers shelled the village, then MUP forces entered the town, looting and burning homes. Again the villagers fled to the woods where they were followed by the -- or found by the MUP and forced to return. The women and children were separated from the men. The men were put into a barn, men including teenagers, mentally and physically disabled, and elderly. Before they were put in a barn they were robbed of their valuables and their identity documents and then they were summarily executed, and the barn was subsequently burned to the ground after it had been set on fire by the MUP. And that's all found at paragraphs 402 to 408 -- or to 409, paragraphs 432 and 1161. These examples are but two of the many instances of crimes committed by VJ and MUP forces over the two-month campaign of violence and terror aimed at driving out the Kosovo Albanian population. The full record of the Trial Chamber's factual findings is found in Volume II from paragraphs 1 to 1178. I won't repeat, as my colleague Ms. Jarvis has taken you to it this morning, paragraph 1178 which is the summary of the factual findings that the Chamber made outlining its conclusions regarding the action. I do just want to point out that in the -- I think penultimate sentence, the Chamber said it was the deliberate actions of these forces during this campaign that caused the departure of at least 700.000 Albanians from Kosovo in the short period of time between the end of March and the beginning of June 1999. The responsibility of the accused has been spoken about for the entire week. Each of them was at a higher level of authority and was responsible for the crimes in Kosovo. Each accused contributed to the commission of crimes in 1999 and for those contributions was found guilty as a JCE member or as an aider and abettor. Given the time, I don't plan to review their contributions. They've been covered several times by both the Prosecution and the Defence, and I'll just close my remarks very briefly by dealing with the error and why it should be corrected. The Chamber erred in imposing sentences, in our submission, that were manifestly inadequate and disproportionate to the crimes committed. If you look at the Chamber's sentencing analysis, you will find that it was cursory and failed to properly account for the certain mandatory factors when assessing the seriousness of crimes. Specifically, the Trial Chamber's analysis on the gravity of offences was limited to six paragraphs and it failed to address the discriminatory nature of crimes and their impact on the victims. And I gave you the illustration of the impact of victims because although I only quoted from two or three, that that is multiplied several hundred thousand times. Indeed, there is virtually no decision on the brutal nature of the crimes or the effects of the crimes on the Kosovo Albanian victims and their relatives. The Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 683, found that these are mandatory considerations when dealing with gravity. The Chamber's cursory sentencing analysis is exemplified by the decision to apportion sentences strictly on the basis of individual criminal liability and the specific mode for which the accused was convicted. The Chamber did not individualise the sentence based on the individual accused's position, his contribution or even the crimes for which he was convicted, which would have been an obvious analysis that would have been required. At Volume III, paragraph 1175 of the judgement, under the heading "Gravity of Crimes," the Chamber erred by taking into account each accused's convicted mode of liability and ignoring specific contributions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, I'm afraid that your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If Your Honour could give me one minute, I assure you I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. And as Your Honour just heard from my colleague Ms. Jarvis, the accused were convicted of different offences. Pavkovic was convicted for sexual offences and our appeal points out that Lukic and Sainovic were acquitted. And the Trial Chamber could have taken this into account. It also could have taken into account the brutality, as I've pointed out, and the fact that each played a distinct, different, and important role but some assessment was required for that. But ultimately the -- the issue is: Were the sentences of 15 years and 22 years respectively for the aider and abettor and the JCE members disproportionate to the seriousness of the crimes? Our submission is that common sense tells you that it was disproportionate. Twenty-two years and 15 years for the size, nature of the crimes, 700 [sic] lives ruined as a result of premeditated and violent actions in a very short time, suggests that particularly given the -- the additional crimes that went along with it in order to promote the violence and terror to get the people to flee justify more severe sentences. In fact, we urge the Chamber to look at imposing the most severe sentences that the Statute allows. Subject to any questions, that would be my remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will have a break and we will resume at 11.00 so as to hear the response from the appellants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are going to hear the response from the appellants. Counsel for Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will address the Honourable Appeals Chamber on the grounds 1 and 3 of the Prosecution appeals brief, while my learned friend Mr. Fila will talk about the 6th ground. Although my learned friends did not address the first ground of their appeal today, I will, however, make two or three points that the Chamber should consider when assessing whether the first ground of appeal of the Prosecution is founded or not. In drafting the third amended indictment which was the basis for all the allegations in this case, the Prosecutor failed to or omitted to as part of ground 5 include the paragraphs which would detail the punishable conduct, and this is paragraph 76, which should have included paragraph 72 describing the acts of deportation and forcible transfer. This was a discernible error on the part of the Prosecution which was noted early on at trial, as early as the 30th of October, 2006. The President of the Trial Chamber drew the attention of the Prosecution to that defect and said that paragraph 76 does not contain the necessary references for paragraph 72 detailing the acts of deportation and forcible transfer. The trial attorney in that case said that he understood what the Trial Chamber meant but had no response to offer, and that was how the discussion ended. Now, the next occasion that the Prosecution had for that same issue was the Trial Chamber's decision on 98 bis, that is to say, the 98 bis decision by the Trial Chamber, which clearly states that the Trial Chamber found that the specific details concerning the deportation and forcible transfer contained in paragraph 72 was simply not included in ground 5 -- in count 5 of the indictment. This was the gist of what the 98 bis decision said. The Prosecution heard that. They had an opportunity to appeal the decision, but that was never done. The first time when the Prosecutor sought to rectify this defect was in the appeal against the trial judgement. In our view, the failure on the part of the Prosecution to intervene in these two -- on these two occasions at trial preclude the Prosecution from the possibility to do so at this appeals stage, to redress this fault on their part which should have been properly addressed at trial. Any intervention at this stage would be directly detrimental and prejudicial for the accused. On this basis, we submit that the Appeals Chamber should dismiss this Prosecution ground of appeal, and I refer you for the details to our reply to the Prosecution brief. With your leave, Your Honours, I'd like to address briefly what was stated here today under ground 3 of the Prosecution appeal, which is divided into two parts. The first one seeks that the legal standard applied be rectified, and the second has to do with the establishment of the circumstances which should lead to a different finding. This refers to the factual findings contained in ground 3. Although mention was made of this matter over the past couple of days, I would like to recall in part what in our understanding are the legal standards that the honourable Chamber should apply in considering this ground of appeal. Regardless of what sort of position the Appeals Chamber will take with regard to the legal standard of foreseeability and possibility, whether they will adhere to the Brdjanin judgement standard or to the position advanced in the interlocutory appeals decision in the Karadzic case, there is another additional part of the standard which the Prosecution does not find needs to be challenged and which in our view gives the gist of the reasoning of this count of appeal. The definition which the Prosecution does not find needs to be challenged as part of JCE III speaks about reasonable foreseeability based on the information available to the accused. Now, this part of definition, information available to the accused, is not to be challenged and in our view is the key issue that can help resolve the situation. What does the Appeals Chamber in the Karadzic case say? They say that regardless of the application of the possibility standard, the requirements cannot be met where there is a scenario of remoteness. The possibility that a crime may be committed must be substantial enough in order to be foreseeable to the accused. What does this clearly state? Well, this clearly states that the Appeals Chamber does not support a comprehensive, limitless definition that the Prosecution advocate. What would be the consequence of the Prosecution's understanding of this matter? Well, that there is a JCE and that there is the mens rea for the common purpose and that any other crime may be qualified or characterized as the crime meeting the requirements for the JCE III. The consequences that stem from the Prosecution's understanding of it is automatism. If there are the requirements and if there is the act of forcible transfer and deportation as the first part of the joint criminal enterprise, the standard has been met according to which the -- automatically where what would be foreseeable would also be the criminal assaults -- the sexual assaults. We believe that there can be no automatism and that, as is the case everywhere else, evidence needs to be identified supporting the decision. If we adopted the concept advanced by the Prosecution, we would slip into automatism and this would preclude the need for these specific crimes to be proven to begin with. Now, as for whether these crimes exist or do not exist, this is something that can be assessed on the basis of the available information. The scenario of remoteness alone cannot suffice to attach responsibility for these crimes to the accused. How do these matters stand with regard to our client, Mr. Sainovic? In explaining these circumstances, at paragraph 472, Volume II, the Trial Chamber concluded that the Prosecution did not adduce evidence which would enable it to find that the sexual assaults were reasonably foreseeable to Sainovic, and what clearly transpires from this paragraph is that the Prosecution -- rather, the Trial Chamber reached its findings by applying the standards from the Kvocka and Krstic cases. In our view, the Trial Chamber assessed these circumstances carefully and based their findings on it. Today our learned friends pointed out the existence of three factors that should serve as evidence: That it had to be reasonably foreseeable to Sainovic that within the alleged campaign that was carried out the acts of sexual assaults would occur, that there was a campaign of fierce violence, and that on the basis of the existence of this campaign, there is foreseeability that these crimes would occur. If we look at the Prosecution appeals brief about Sainovic's knowledge of this campaign of fierce violence, we will find several statements only referring to 1998, the events at Gornje Obrinje, the events at Racak, the events at Malisevo. However, all those events, and this is something that we address in detail in our reply, clearly indicate that there was no sexual violence and that there was nothing that could lead to the conclusion that there might have occurred such crimes. However, the Prosecutor makes a contradictory statement. Most of the submissions we heard from the Prosecution over the past several days were based on allegations that there was something that existed in 1998, and that this something that existed in 1998 could therefore only and exclusively exist in 1999. As for the evidence in relation to 1998, there was nothing that would point to any sort of crime that may be related to sexual violence. We provided our detailed reasoning of this in writing, and I believe that my learned friend Madam Prosecutor conceded that on the basis of the knowledge from 1998, the accused could not have this sort of anticipation. If we were to accept this logic of the Prosecution, if year 1998 were indeed a warning, a basis for such knowledge, then it's clear that Nikola Sainovic did not have that warning, and it cannot be established that that type of crime could have been foreseeable based on what he knew from the time before, before the JCE began. The Prosecution mention in their brief and also today the strong animosity between Serbs and Albanians as an indication that all types of violence, including this type of violence, were all possible, but we do not find this in information available in 1998. The Prosecution establishes violence in 1998. They link it with 1999. However, this type of violence did not exist in 1998. The question of animosity is an issue between Serbs and Albanians in Kosovo that goes back decades, perhaps longer. But the history of the region shows that this animosity does not include the acts discussed here. What is especially curious is the OTP mentions that Sainovic could have assumed that if the same units were in Kosovo that had been present in Bosnia and elsewhere years before, they could commit the same type of act in Kosovo. It is a big question what exactly Sainovic knew about which units were engaged, what they had done before. This is a claim that something could be foreseen based on the broadest knowledge of the history in the former Yugoslavia. In the opinion of this Defence, this foreseeability based on general history is not carry an argument that carries any weight in these proceedings. The Prosecution mentions again today that Sainovic was in Pristina on several occasions. They mention two dates, 29th March and 4th April. That he was able to see displacements and transfers and could have, based on that, foreseen sexual assault. There is no evidence about what Sainovic had seen. This is all based on assumptions. But what could illustrate the state of mind of Sainovic is that he was in Pristina on these dates in order to negotiate with Mr. Rugova to try to find a political solution for the problems in Kosovo. Linking his visits and his attempts to resolve the situation through negotiations with what he might have seen is something we have no evidence of, and this Defence believes it is completely inappropriate. We therefore believe that the honourable Appeals Chamber should reject the third ground of appeal by the Prosecution. If I may only mention two more things within my time limit. Of course, the Defence of Mr. Sainovic believes that every act of sexual violence is heinous and deserves the harshest punishment, but we believe also that all the evidence shows that Mr. Sainovic has absolutely nothing to do with such acts. However, it is also necessary to emphasise that the Prosecution speaks of a campaign that lasts for days, weeks, for months, throughout Kosovo, a campaign that involves over 700.000 people. What do we have in terms of facts concerning sexual assaults? There are two acts, and we do not dispute their weight. We're just emphasising the number. The first one is the 29th March, 1999, in Beleg, and the other is in mid-April in Cirez. It is obvious that these are isolated crimes. It is obvious that if it is true that hundreds of thousands of people were involved, we have two incidents involving eight victims. This is not to diminish the suffering of the victims, but this is an indication of the isolated and sporadic character of these incidents. The isolated and sporadic character of the incidents refutes the claim of the Prosecution that Sainovic, together with the others accused of being involved in the JCE, could have foreseen these acts of sexual violence. And very briefly concerning the fourth ground of appeal. Three incidents are involved. Our position is that these incidents show no discriminatory intent, that the Prosecution is trying to copy-paste the general characterization of the attacks on these incidents of violence and that these incidents belong in the category of general crime, certainly not crime with discriminatory intent, and there is no basis, absolutely none whatsoever, for accepting this ground of the Prosecution's appeal. Thank you very much, Your Honours. Mr. Fila will take over now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, Judges. I shall deal with the part of the Prosecution appeal which in my eyes is impermissible and, among other things, immoral. The reason is this: At trial, the Prosecution spent two years in prosecution with us and the Trial Chamber. We saw every witness, every document. We saw the conduct of the accused, and when all this was over, the appeal brief of the Prosecution asked for at least 20 years' sentence for Milosevic [as interpreted], Sainovic, and others. Milutinovic, as you know, was acquitted, but Sainovic was sentenced to 22 years, which is the required sentence plus two years. I want to tell you one thing. I'm probably the oldest lawyer before this Tribunal.
