I've been here since February 1996 - I think Prosecutor Mark Harmon is the only one who's been here longer - and I've never seen anything like this. I want to tell you, and I'm proud of this, that the co-operation we had here between the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Trial Chamber is absolutely unprecedented. Let me show you two examples that was in private session, a discussion between the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. If you want to allow me to do this, we would have to move into private session. If not, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did I mention these two examples? Because I wanted to present to the Appeals Chamber the meaning of promise. What does a colleague's and lawyer's word mean if they appear before this Tribunal? If we were to say one thing and do another, we would be politicians. We would be sitting in the Assembly where nobody knows what other people are saying or what they are -- what they mean. This is a serious Tribunal. What did we gain instead of -- of the consistency? Milutinovic was acquitted. He didn't get 20 years. He didn't get life. Can there be -- is there an appeal against that? No. Ojdanic got 15. The Prosecutor appealed and had the right to do that because the sentence is for under 20 years, and what happened? They gave up on that appeal. This is another situation that you have to have in mind. And the first situation is the one that I'm in with Sainovic. They got what they wanted, and they appealed. I'm not contesting the part of the appeal that has nothing to do with sentencing. I'm not contesting that. They have the right to appeal. What I am saying here is that the parties to these proceedings are bound by their positions which they present during the case. If a party to the proceedings voices a position, they have to adhere to that. Every aberration from any such position introduces elements of legal insecurity into the whole proceedings. That's why I read the Prosecutor's answer about the interview. You know very well that the accused in the proceedings have the right to be aware of the indictment against him. They have the right to be informed about their position. They have the right to adjust their defence to the nature of the indictment and all the other allegations against him. If the Prosecution acts based on the evidence and their own legal position with regard to sentencing, then the Prosecution does that based on their assessment of the evidence, and I am emphasising the word "their own," because in -- in the proceedings, the Prosecution asked for that sentence because they thought that the entire indictment will be taken into account and will be the grounds for sentencing. And this didn't happen. I cannot imagine as a Defence counsel that the Prosecution, based on the same evidence, because no other new evidence was presented here, and the same legal theory during one phase of the procedure asked for one sentence and then in another phase of the procedure without any evidence and about -- any changes with regard to the position of the accused, they want another sentence. This is not fair. This is not professional. This is not how colleagues act. This is not in keeping with our joint obligation to serve justice and respect the rights of all the parties to the proceedings, meaning the accused and the victims, the Defence, and the Prosecution. Any aberration from the original position that the Prosecution presented during the first instance case now, in this phase of the procedure, has to be based on other evidence or drastically change legal practice. How is it possible for somebody who did not see those people, who did not see the case file -- or, rather, saw only the case file and has only indirect knowledge about what was going on during the two years can see better than the Prosecutor who was here. Two of the members of that first instance Prosecutor's office are now here, Mr. Marcussen and Ms. Kravetz, and it seems that they have changed their opinion in the meantime. You know, in the law that I practice in my own country before the Special Tribunal which is a Tribunal that tries the cases of drug trafficking, corruption, and other grave crimes, the Prosecutor asks for a certain sentence, and when they receive that sentence, they do not have the right to appeal. It has never happened. They can appeal if they don't like a formulation, the kind of wording, but if they were given the sentencing that they requested, they can't appeal. How is that possible here? I looked at everything that has been written. We compared it with what the first instance panel wrote. What is it that the Trial Chamber didn't see and the Prosecution sitting here before us did see? Everything is there. They presented tables to our appeals brief. This is what it says in the sentence. This is what it says in the judgement. Let them make their own table as to what they say and what is in the judgement. If they see any differences and discrepancies, fine, we don't have a problem. I'm really concerned you know. At the beginning of indictments for Kosovo, which, unfortunately, apply only to Serbs, there were three politicians besides Sainovic who were accused. Slobodan Milosevic who died in prison because he was indicted the way he was, and he could not stand such a long trial. I remind you of Judge May's words who wanted only Kosovo to be indicted. And the second one is Milan Milutinovic who was acquitted. The third one was Vlajko Stojilkovic who was the minister of the interior in Serbia. He killed himself. And now the only -- or, rather, Slobodan Milosevic died before he could be tried, presumed innocent. Milutinovic was acquitted. It is especially interesting in the position of this Prosecution that Milutinovic was acquitted and they do not appeal. Of all the responsible politicians who were mentioned in the judgement, only Sainovic remains, and now all of a sudden the Prosecutor wants a different sentence, life in this case. They want that to be laid -- to be handed down on Sainovic. You know, you have in the Bible a story about a goat that the Jews took to the wolves to be eaten and that all the sins will go away with that. I believe that Sainovic is in the same position, that he is supposed to take the blame for everything that was not done or remains unresolved. You see, Serbia has the police. Serbia has the government. The government has the minister of the interior. It has the prime minister. Serbia has the president of the republic. How come that one of the vice-prime ministers in the government, as the Prosecutor alleges, knows everything and the person in charge of the police hasn't a clue about all that, or the president? This is not fair. This is not humane. It is not fair to impute to the only one person that remains everything that the Prosecution failed to do successfully with other people. That's why we hear today that the MUP commander -- instead of imputing on Sainovic what Milutinovic was supposed to be charged with, why are we doing that? Why do we have to blame Sainovic for the sins of Milutinovic? Vlajko Stojilkovic was in command only of the MUP, not only of the state security. He was in command, but he was not so powerful to be involved in war operations and do everything, whereas the president of the Republic of Serbia was sitting clueless in a bunker next door to Slobodan Milosevic. Slobodan Milosevic and his wife, and the other guy and his wife, and above them was the Supreme Staff that was allegedly planning operations unbeknownst to them. I have learned that if somebody says something - I repeat this once again - if somebody says something, if somebody promises something, they're bound by their words. Here one man is taking the role of another one. Milutinovic's exculpated together with the others and they are replaced by Sainovic who is supposed to take their blame. One day somebody will wonder how come that the Prosecutor kept a person in gaol for seven years. They ask life sentence for him. He is acquitted and they don't appeal. When you look at the records of this trial, you will see that I did not stop in my defence of Sainovic. Every day Prosecutor had something to lay against -- against Sainovic but not against Milutinovic. The proceedings was run in the way as if everybody knew what the final outcome was going to be. It was in a way tepid. It was not carried out energetically. If the Prosecutor - and let me repeat one more time - if the Prosecutor in this case based on the evidence available to them and their legal understanding of the sentencing, they will ask for a sentence based on their assessment of the evidence available to them. And now let me deal with the appeal itself. The Prosecutor does not present any new arguments that would justify any aberrations from the position that they had in the first instance case. The Prosecutor, when asking for 20 years for Sainovic, bore in mind a number of facts for which they deemed that they represent very important evidence on Sainovic's guilt and sentence, and that those aggravated his position with regard to the responsibility of the crimes that he was charged with. This is what the Prosecution claim, that Sainovic obstructed the application of the October agreement. He refused the entry of the inspection into the barracks. He did not allow the KLA helicopter to enter Kosovo, that he turned down the proposal that the forces in Malisevo should be reduced, and that the KLA should be deployed in order to -- and he also allowed -- he obstructed negotiations in Rambouillet. All of these allegations in the judgement of the Trial Chamber which -- with which we are not satisfied have been rejected. None of these allegations were accepted by the Trial Chamber in the first instance proceedings. And now in a very paradoxical way, the Prosecutor is asking for a higher sentence for Sainovic in a situation which is even more favourable for Sainovic than at the time when the Prosecutor asked for a sentence of 20-plus years for Sainovic. The reasons of fairness impose the rejection of that request on the part of the Prosecutor. In addition to that, the Prosecutor did not present any serious reason why the sentence as has been pronounced is not unfair. And let me now talk about the 700.000 Albanians whose lives were ruined because they were not at home for a month. 120.000 Serbs who had been chased away from Kosovo before that and they are still in Serbia, and those who remain in Kosovo die every day. Has anybody been charged with that? No. It is not very difficult to explain the situation of the Albanians -- to the Albanians with indictments against the Serbs, but how can we explain the situation to the Serbs who fled before NATO bombing and there are 120.000 of us living in Serbia? This is all of what I wanted to say and I apologise for being so emotional at moments. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that we will hear the reply this afternoon by the Prosecution on this very issue. Now for the response by the counsel for Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I expect to be quite brief this morning, take up very little time, partly because my colleagues said some of the things that I intended to say. The Prosecution is before you this morning asking you to save them from themselves in a couple of instances, that they made prior decisions and now they've decided they don't like those prior decisions they made so they want you to let them change those decisions. It reminds me of when I wanted some more time to argue my client's case here and you told me, well, you made that prior decision that you didn't want that time or you would have let us know earlier. And so, you know, I'm in the same position they are, and what I got, they should get too, it seems to me. The first one of those, of course, is when they deliberately decided, in the face of Judge Bonomy's almost pleading with them, not to amend paragraph 76 of the indictment to include the allegations in paragraph 72, they made that decision, and now after the effect of that, they want you to let them reverse that and you consider it as if they had amended the indictment. You shouldn't do that. And we argue, of course, that there was a waiver and I think it's clearly a waiver. The ground that I want to talk about now is that from ground 4 dealing with the sexual assaults which I talked with you at some length about in answer to the Court's questions, and so I will rely primarily what I said then and what we say in our brief. However, I really must comment on what we heard this morning. We need to understand that the prerequisite to the sexual assault issues that are the subject of ground 4 is that there must have been proof of a JCE I beyond reasonable doubt. We say there was not, that even though a JCE can be shown by circumstantial evidence, it's not sufficient that it is a reasonable conclusion available from that evidence but that it is the only reasonable conclusion available from the evidence. And we think it was not. And there's a lot of evidence to show that it was not. The evidence of -- that I mentioned the other day of a number of refugees that were at the border trying to cross and the VJ forces said, No, you go back to your homes. We'll help you, we'll feed you. They did. The chaos of war provides an opportunity for the criminally inclined who might be disguised as military personnel to engage in all kinds of criminal acts. It's essential that the evidence identify the perpetrators of these crimes that were talked about this morning as persons over whom the accused have control. The Prosecution could not identify the perpetrators of these rapes. We don't know who they were. We don't know if they were ever identified and punished, or if they're alive or walking this earth somewhere free. We just don't know. The Prosecutor needs to make that identification before it can ask that General Pavkovic be held responsible for what those persons did. They must prove that not only were they under his control but that he did not make sufficient efforts to prevent, and if not prevent it did not make sufficient efforts to see that they were identified and punished. Commanders in any war, no matter how hard they try, cannot prevent the commission of crimes. They just happen. They must try and when they fail, these -- then sufficient efforts must be made to punish. I want to go very briefly into the sentencing issue. Clearly there were serious crimes committed in Kosovo in 1999, but it is not the number and the character of those crimes that is important to the issue of sentencing but the identity of the perpetrators and their connection to General Pavkovic. When the OTP was not able to identify perpetrators in the crimes, they simply referred to them as VJ and MUP forces which is not any kind of an identification at all. What they're saying when they say "VJ and MUP forces," is that we can't tell you whether these people were with the VJ or with the MUP. We don't know who they were, so we'll just call them forces of FRY and Serbia. We just don't know who they were. And that's endemic in this case, Your Honours. You look at all the crime base in this case. There's no firm identification of the people who were committing the crimes that were being committed. The second time that the Prosecution has asked you to save them from themselves is when this morning, after having gotten what they asked for sentence-wise, they're now asking you, well, we're sorry, we didn't like what we got from what we asked last time. Let's try again. If you look at the transcript, 26947, in closing arguments in the case, you can see Prosecutor Hannis saying, "We'd like a sentence of at least 20 years." Well, they got more than that. They got 22 for my guy. And now they're saying, no, that wasn't enough, and Mr. Hannis was wrong, and please save us from ourselves. A life sentence is not a reasonable sentence. I think sentencing should not be an issue due to the flawed character of this judgement. It is so factually flawed that sentencing shouldn't even arise as a question. It should be remembered that Pavkovic provided documents to this Tribunal including the minutes of the Joint Command meetings. He had nothing to hide. He gave an interview to the OTP before he was indicted. He co-operated in the investigation for which he received no credit in the judgement to mitigate that, and you'll see that at paragraph 364 of our main brief. That's all I have to tell you this morning, Your Honours. I appreciate your attention, and I think our brief filed in response to the Prosecutor's main brief covers everything else that's important. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that concludes your response. Thank you very much, especially for your briefness. I think it's time for us to have a lunch break. We will resume at 1.30 this afternoon, at 1.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We will continue the response from the appellants. Counsel for Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will try to provide answers or to respond to some of the submissions that my learned friends indicated in their appeal which concern General Lazarevic, those that they mentioned in their brief and those that they mentioned in their oral submissions today. Our Defence appealed or challenged the first ground of appeal of the Prosecution by maintaining that the Prosecution is wrong in claiming that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that -- in acquitting Ojdanic and Lazarevic of aiding and abetting murder. Our Defence joins the submissions made by my learned friend Mr. Petrovic, who spoke earlier today about the failure on the part of the Prosecution to relate all the material aspects relating to this -- to these acts in the indictment. I would here like to refer the Appeals Chamber to the other reasons we provided in our reply to the appeal brief which can be found at paragraphs 5 through 16 of our reply to the Prosecution brief. I would now like to address the second ground of appeal of the Prosecution, which is the one that they addressed orally earlier today where they presented their views and arguments supporting the position that General Lazarevic should have been convicted of aiding and abetting in the crime of murder. In our view, the Trial Chamber did not err in acquitting General Lazarevic of aiding and abetting murder. The Prosecutor spoke of the specific direction standard again today, which is an issue that was discussed the day before yesterday when we were presenting our appeal and the Prosecution were giving their reply. Should you apply a reasonable standard of specific direction, in that case it would be quite clear and unequivocally so from the totality of evidence that General Lazarevic cannot be responsible for aiding and abetting murder. Although I am fully convinced that it is quite justified and legitimate to apply the specific directions standard to General Lazarevic, even if we were to disregard that principle, still there are ample reasons to acquit General Lazarevic of this crime. In other words, in keeping with the Trial Chamber's finding acquitting him of that responsibility. We heard submissions today that for aiding and abetting murder, the sufficient standard would have been that General Lazarevic was aware of the probability or the likelihood that murders would occur. I believe that this is an impermissibly broad interpretation of the standard, because in that case any participant in a war could automatically be thought to have the mens rea that murders are likely to happen. In any war situation, improper conduct may occur, including murder. That is precisely why preventative orders were issued by General Lazarevic, and this is the very purpose of the criminal reports that were filed against the perpetrators of crimes before the relevant judiciary bodies. In our view, the standard there was reason that he knew which could be applied under Article 3 [as interpreted] of the Statute, whereas when we speak of individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1), there, at the very least, the accused must be aware of the fact that his action or omission may assist the perpetrators in the commission of crimes. The Prosecution did not succeed in proving that this standard was met either. I would like to now address the specific locations that my learned friend from the Prosecution spoke of. Your Honours, my colleague tells me that we have Article 3 of the Statute as recorded in the transcript whereas I referred to Article 7(3), and I'm referring to page 63, line 7. Your Honours, with your leave I'd like to briefly discuss the locations mentioned by my learned friend which were not found beyond a reasonable doubt, absolutely not, as places where General Lazarevic aided and abetted murder. The Trial Chamber quite rightly found that none of the evidence adduced proved that General Lazarevic was aware that the MUP or VJ forces were going into the specific crime sites in order to commit killings. Specifically, my learned friend mentioned Korenica and Meja in the Djakovica municipality. The evidence shows that the VJ did not participate in the incidents in and around Korenica and Meja on the 27th of April, 1999, in the municipality of Djakovica, and the case presented by the Prosecution was merely speculation, because there was no evidence to support it. The Defence maintains that in that area there was a large presence of the KLA in the relevant period when the event happened, and this is what the combat report of the 125th Brigade of the 25th of April, 1999, attests to. And I refer you to P2023. We also heard witness Nik Peraj, a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, who in no uncertain terms said that in the Reka Valley, where this action was carried out in Meja and Korenica, there was a strong presence of the 137th Brigade of the KLA. And I refer you to P2252, paragraph 105. The report of the 125th Brigade was P2023. Prosecution witness Bislim Zyrapi, the Chief of Staff of the KLA, said that the KLA used heavy artillery from the territory of Albania in order to provide fire support to its units in the Reka Valley starting from the 9th of April, 1999. Therefore, the speculations advanced by the Prosecution were not true, that there was an action carried out with the intent of driving out women -- civilians, women, children, and persons in wheelchairs. There is ample evidence which, at least alternatively, may lead to a reasonable inference that the action carried out in the Reka Valley had the aim of resisting a strong activity on the part of the KLA including that of its heavy artillery from the territory of Albania. And I refer you here to transcript pages 6238 to 6239. There is ample evidence to show that in Korenica and Meja, that is to say, the Djakovica municipality, there was a strong KLA presence and that the action carried out in Korenica and Meja was a military action directed against the KLA. Another important issue is that in the case file there is no evidence to show that General Lazarevic was informed that there were killings of civilians occurring in that action. There is no evidence to support that. There is also no -- there is also evidence to show that in the area of Djakovica there was a forward command post where there was Colonel Zivkovic who assigned tasks to the 125th Brigade to hold a stretch of the front line without advancing further. In other words, there is no evidence that General Lazarevic issued any sort of order in respect of this action. Let me move on to a different location now. My time is running out quickly. This is Dubrava/Lisnaja. Your Honours, there you will also find ample evidence which fully and unequivocally justify the position of the Trial Chamber that General Lazarevic was not responsible for this incident of killing. There are killings of two Kosovo Albanians in Dubrava and Kacanik municipality on the 25th of May, and there is ample evidence to show that this was not committed by the VJ. Secondly, there is no evidence to show that General Lazarevic had any knowledge of this incident. We have heard witness Krsman Jelic testify. He was the commander of the unit who was present in that area. He was the commander of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. According to his testimony, there was a strong presence of the KLA in the area. The inhabitants of the village left their village of their own free will and left for Macedonia. General Krsman Jelic made markings on the map where he clearly showed what the positions of the army were and where the fighting against the KLA took place. And I refer you here to Exhibit P370, pages of the transcript 19146. The evidence will indicate clearly that there was fighting going on between the KLA and the VJ in the area. You will also see that none of the reports and documents put General Lazarevic on notice of the fact that there was anything improper going on in the area, especially not the killing of the civilians. Your Honours, the Prosecutor said when addressing the standard, which as we already submitted was very low, General Lazarevic had to have known based on the events from 1998 that these killings might occur in 1999. I wish to draw your attention to the documentation that I mentioned the day before yesterday, which was on quite a different set of events and in respect of the fact that, in 1998, the situation on the ground and the situation with regard to General Lazarevic's position was completely different, and this must be taken into consideration with the other factors that we mentioned. In 1998, General Lazarevic was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps and was present at the forward command post in Djakovica. He was securing the state border facing Albania from where there was a high inflow of weapons and personnel on an almost daily basis. General Lazarevic was erroneously described as a person who was mentioned -- who was present when General Samardzic, who was the corps commander then, or, rather, the 3rd Army commander, had a meeting with the Pristina Corps commander. This is Exhibit Number 4D97, which clearly shows that General Lazarevic was not present in that meeting. When the Chief of Staff was mentioned, what was meant was the 3rd Army Chief of Staff, because he was also the signatory. Please look closely at 4D97 and you will see this discernible error that General Lazarevic indeed was not present at the meeting which discussed torching. Also, with regard to 1999, the Prosecution cites the example where General Lazarevic, considering that he was in Pristina at the time, should have known that in addition to deportations there were also killings of Albanian civilians. This claim by the Prosecution is also a speculation, an example of speculation that does not rely on any evidence at all. From the case file you will see that the command post of the Pristina Corps from the beginning of the bombing was never in the town of Pristina. The command post was several kilometres outside of Pristina at a place called Kisnica, and there are numerous exhibits to prove this. Defence witness Filipovic also testified in great detail to the fact that there were no units, no troops of the VJ in Pristina itself. Your Honours, this makes the claim from the Prosecution appeal that General Lazarevic should have had such knowledge because he was in Pristina for a meeting on 19 April 1999 completely unreasonable, mere speculation. You will see if you look at this meeting that it was late at night and that General Lazarevic came to Pristina for that meeting at 1.00 a.m. from his command post in Kisnica for one hour only. And let me recall that by that time, 600.000 out of the total of 700.000 Albanians had already been deported. So it is absurd to claim that based on that one-hour meeting in Pristina, General Lazarevic had reason to know that in addition to deportations of civilian population there were also killings. Your Honours, I will now let my colleague Mr. Cepic address the Prosecution grounds of appeal 5 and 6 and present our arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this opportunity, Your Honour. As my colleague Mr. Bakrac said, I will address the Prosecution grounds of appeal 5 and 6 and attempt to respond to the submissions of our learned friend Mr. Kremer. We have already addressed the issue of deportations from Urosevac, Zabare, and Prizren, Dusanovo. I will not come back to that except to say that these allegations do not correspond to what the Prosecution say, and the Trial Chamber was correct in finding that General Lazarevic had nothing to do with the incidents in that area, also a plethora of evidence has been adduced, diaries of various brigades and other units active in that area. We have pointed out to inconsistencies in witness testimonies considering Staro -- Sojevo, Misojevo [phoen] and other places in that municipality, including Zabarevo [phoen]. Speaking of deportations and forced transfers in Zabrezje, I would like to recall that witnesses themselves confirmed that in this place, there was a military hospital of the KLA. [In English] And that was confirmed by the Prosecutor witness Mahmut Halimi, transcript page 4447, 4448, which clearly demonstrate to us that it was a strong -- stronghold of KLA in that village. That means that we could use the pattern which is clearly described by the Prosecutor witness, credible Prosecutor witness, Chief of Staff Bislim Zyrapi who said that: "It was normal for us to order the movement of population but also of the KLA." Also, I would like to add something more regarding to that issue. My learned friend Mr. Kremer today on the page of transcript 37 explained alleged crimes on the space of Orahovac municipality, quoted places Celine and Pirane on 25th of March, 1999. I have to again quote Chief of Staff of KLA, page of transcript 5992: "... in the area starting from Pirane and up to Gjakova junction and Bellacerkva, the attacks were launched early in the morning on 25th of March, there was combat activity. "I want to mention this: Before the artillery attack started -- correction. After the artillery attack started, we wanted the population in this area to move out for security reasons. The KLA forces, together with the population began to withdraw." So that means with this piece of evidence in corroboration with other direct evidence that on that place at that time was very strong combat activities between VJ and MUP from one side and KLA from another side. I would also like to draw your attention that on other areas out of alleged crime base, there is no evidence, no allegation about alleged deportation or forcible transfer. For example, nearest to village Nogavac, which is just couple hundred metres from Celine, was attacked by NATO bomb on 2nd of April, 1999, and Trial Chamber found that there is no crimes regarding to that location. That is the same area, almost the same period of time, but completely different reason for the movement of population. Prosecutor in his appeal brief also marked that VJ forces allegedly committed crimes in suburb of Prizren, Dusanovo. One of Prosecutor witnesses testified that on 28th of March, 1999, there was about 50 tanks and military units of VJ. During the morning, my learned friend Mr. Kremer explained that VJ unit 449th Brigade was in the area of Orahovac. That was the only combat unit in that area. So it is not possible to be at two places at the same time. Also report from that brigade from 30th of March, P195, clearly describes positions and movements of VJ units. I would like to present you piece of evidence which is taken just couple streets from Dusanovo area, in Prizren town, in April 1999. I kindly ask my assistant to play Exhibit Number 5D1374. With sound, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The entire video clip is about four minutes, so I kindly ask my assistant just to play couple inserts from it. From this video-clip you can see the distortion of buildings. You can see civilians, Albanian civilians, from their clothing it is very simple to [indiscernible] that. You can see VJ members assisting civilians. Also see the units, civil protection units. So thank you very much. So the reasonable question is: Who can remain on that location after this distortion [sic]? Even before, even later. Request of Prosecutor for the sentence regarding to General Lazarevic is completely unfounded. That request is not founded with any clear explanation. The sentence of 15 years' imprisonment for aiding and abetting is too high. The Defence disposition has established that in this case, the Trial Chamber didn't take into account all relevant pieces of evidence, especially the facts that General Lazarevic was the first one who gave the interview as accused, that General Lazarevic was the only one who testified before the Trial Chamber, even before any of Defence witnesses, and also many of evidence which clearly shows intention and activities of General Lazarevic to provide humanitarian aid to civilians in difficult wartime period. We're just explaining that to illustrate situation, that the request of Prosecutor is completely unfounded. For all those reasons, we kindly request from this honourable Appeals Chamber to dismiss Prosecutor appeal. And I kindly ask for one correction in transcript page 70, line 16. It has to be "destruction" instead of "distortion." Thank you very much for your attention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think there's one question I would like to ask. I would like to seek your clarification on your position that that is to your understanding of the judgement, what kind of legal criteria the Trial Chamber applied concerning of the aiding and abetting? I mean, the Trial Chamber applied the specific direction criteria or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, we believe that the Trial Chamber did not apply the criterion of specific direction and that is why they indeed convicted General Lazarevic of aiding and abetting, deportation and forcible transfer. We believe that even applying the inappropriate milder standard, the criteria for mens rea would not have been met and General Lazarevic should not be convicted. What we were trying to say that by applying the standard of specific direction, the inadequacy of the conviction of General Lazarevic for this would be even more obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that later on I will also seek the positions or understandings of the Prosecution in this matter. I think that is all the questions, so may we hear the counsel for Mr. Lukic's reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thank you for the opportunity to address you in relation to the Prosecution's appeal on behalf of Mr. Lukic. At the outset I'd like to tell you that if there's anything that we have mentioned in our response brief which we do not present to you here today orally, that does not mean that we are withdrawing any of the arguments that we wrote in there. We are simply trying to highlight some points within the time period that Your Honours have granted us. I would like to start by noting that the Prosecution appeal essentially in every ground is merely seeking different ways to seek and obtain an increase of the sentence which was initially requested by the Prosecution at trial and which was imposed against Mr. Lukic by the Trial Chamber. As you heard from our Defence yesterday, the sentencing of our client to a 22-year sentence is manifestly unjust and in error for multiple reasons, the foremost one being an inappropriate treatment of the evidence of mitigation. I will not repeat those arguments today, but I ask that you please bear them in mind when considering the Prosecution appeal. I must also remark respectfully that this Prosecution appeal violates fundamental issues of fairness and the most basic appellate principles. Your Honours, a party is not permitted to appeal from its own mistake. The Prosecution received the sentence within the range that it asked for and should be barred by the doctrine of estoppel from seeking a higher sentence on appeal. Surely in seeking a sentence of at least 20 years at the conclusion of their case the Prosecution at that time had in mind all the appropriate standards of proof as well as the entirety of their evidence, and thus, the sentence that they sought at that time was what they believed was appropriate under the standards of proof and the evidence. Thus, Your Honours, I submit irrespective of whether the Trial Chamber made any errors or not in relation to the standards of proof for JCE III, irrespective of the other grounds of appeal that the Prosecution has raised in this appeal, the Prosecution cannot claim that those errors call for an increase in sentence since they, the Prosecution, were aware of the correct standards, as they say, were aware of their evidence and still asked for a sentence of no less than 20 years and got a sentence of no less than 20 years. In fact, more, 22. The Prosecution has failed to cite to any legal authority that permits them after having prevailed at trial to now seek a second bite of the apple and appeal against their own error, the Prosecution's error, not any error by the Chamber in sentencing. Such a position turns the appellate process on its head. The Prosecution's request that sentencing be based on a simple quantitative calculation would amount to retribution without restraint and would be contrary to the sentencing principles of the Tribunal. It should be recalled that an integral part of the principle of retribution is restraint which requires a fair and balanced approach based upon the culpability of the individual defendant. The Appeals Chamber has stated clearly that retribution must not be accorded undue prominence in sentencing. The Aleksovski appeal judgement at paragraph 185 stands for that proposition. What is clear in the jurisprudence is that concern for the principles of retribution and deterrence cannot justify a departure from the fundamental principles that an individual should be punished solely on the basis of his wrongdoing. This is paragraph 64 of the Nikolic appeal judgement. Thus, in applying the sentencing principles, the limits of sentences are necessarily set by the prior assessment of the gravity of the offence properly taking into account the precise conduct of the accused. The Prosecution position wishes to focus only on the gravity of the offence for which the trial judgement found Lukic liable, and we say that the trial judgement is in error finding him liable, but the Prosecution wishes only to focus on that without applying the second half of the test, which is an analysis of the integral role or lack thereof of the accused. In this regard, it ought to be stressed that under the prior case law of the Tribunal, gradations of fault within the JCE doctrine are possible and may be reflected in the sentences given. This was a finding of the Krajisnik trial judgement at paragraph 886. I implore the members of this panel and this Chamber to use their common sense and legal training to reject the Prosecution's calls for a higher sentence irrespective of the outcome of the remainder of their appeal. Now I wish to turn to some of the other submissions of my learned colleagues from the Prosecution. Today we heard submissions about the crimes of sexual assaults and the claim of the Prosecution that they were foreseeable under the JCE possibility standard since armed security forces and soldiers were out and about during the period of NATO bombings. As the Appeals Chamber in Karadzic has stated, it is worth noting that the term "possibility standard" is not satisfied by implausibly remote scenarios plotted on a spectrum of likelihood. The JCE III mens rea standard does not require an understanding that a deviatory crime would probably be committed. It does, however, require that the possibility a crime could be committed is sufficiently substantial as to be foreseeable to an accused. That's paragraph 18 of the Karadzic decision that is the basis of the Prosecution's appeal. Thus, Your Honours, the appropriate analysis focuses on what was foreseeable and substantially known to the accused under the set of facts he operated under at the time. So we need to look at the set of facts, not the Prosecution's characterization of them. It is important to note that even though the Prosecution is no longer claiming the evidence that they cited shows actual notice as to Mr. Lukic, you should still look at the same because that evidence the Prosecution has cited relates to separate isolated opportunistic acts and not what the Prosecution is now claiming. Under such a factual backdrop, the possibility such crimes were foreseeable is not sufficiently substantial so as to permit a conviction of Lukic. By way of example, the Prosecution relies upon evidence of individual crimes of sexual assault that were not shown to have occurred during any joint VJ-MUP actions but, rather, were individual instances of crime that were investigated and punished by the proper law enforcement authorities, be they police or military police. I would urge Your Honours to look at appendix 1 of the OTP appeal brief and check all those instances. I ask the panel to consider when individual opportunistic sexual assaults occur during a time of armed conflict and when perpetrators are arrested and processed by either the military police or the civilian police of that state, what more can a state official, in this case Mr. Lukic, have done? I must take the time to draw your attention again to the lack of any disciplinary authority Lukic had in his position as head of the MUP staff. Yesterday, the Prosecution suggested he could indirectly cause SUP chiefs to institute disciplinary proceedings. I want to present you with a citation to the evidence of what in fact a former SUP chief and an OTP insider witness, Mr. Cvetic, actually said at transcript page 8152 through 8153. If you look there you will see that he says SUPs could only proceed with disciplinary actions upon consent from the police administration in Belgrade. The MUP staff had no say in this process. So, Your Honours, Lukic had no disciplinary authority over disciplinary proceedings of MUP members. In any event, he had no actual notice of sexual assaults let alone any committed by MUP members. Under what basis in law, under what basis in equity should he be found liable and punished for these same crimes? I ask Your Honours: Do we really want to establish a strict liability standard that would hold anyone in a state official position culpable of rape or sexual assaults committed by unknown others either without any actual forewarning that such things could occur simply because there is a state of war underway and the chaos of war is afoot, particularly when it is a war that they neither asked for nor started? We submit this is too remote. We submit that the Prosecution is asking for the standard to be diluted beyond that which has actually been established by the jurisprudence. And, Your Honours, we would say that the presumption of guilt is not permitted in criminal proceedings. We ask you to repel this part of the Prosecution appeal. The Prosecution at paragraph 53 of their reply and in the paragraphs contained in ground 4 of their appeal state that Lukic knew of crimes in 1998 and crimes and expulsion of Kosovo Albanians in 1999 due to his leadership role in the MUP. Arising out of the Prosecution's leadership argument is the presumption that Lukic had detailed information about activities and crimes so as to provide substantial knowledge forecasting the possibility of sexual assaults. This is at paragraph 68 of the OTP's appeal brief. We have analysed in our appeal brief the lack of reporting as to the anti-terrorist actions, the lack of information available after NATO began its air-strikes, and other factors relating to the ability or inability of Lukic to have information from the field. For instance, that could be seen in our appeal paragraphs 641 through 683. They are instructive, I think, for this analysis as well. The Prosecution in this ground attempts to rely on information contained in meetings of the so-called Joint Command and to draw improper conclusions there from to illustrate Lukic's reported knowledge of crimes. However, when you look at what they cite, for instance, book 3, paragraphs 1080 and 1081 of the judgement, what is being discussed at those meetings were actually unverified information from various sources of rumours of a crime that had not yet been legally confirmed to be a crime, that is the respective Prosecutor's office with jurisdiction over the same had not conducted investigations, but a review of the record shows that the authorities diligently followed up and investigated even unverified information in accord with the law. I would direct you to P948, page 159; 6D613; 6D1631, paragraphs 27 through 31, 60 and 93. The misapprehension of the evidence on the part of the Prosecution appeal continues at paragraph 70, where it is again asserted that Lukic was well informed of crimes at meetings where these crimes were discussed. However, a look at these paragraphs from the judgement and the underlying evidence also shows no crimes being discussed. Indeed, paragraph 1079 and 1081 of the judgement that are cited in this paragraph have no mention of crimes. The reference to paragraphs dealing with Sainovic at book 3, 442 and 463, only demonstrate discussion of the, quote/unquote, humanitarian catastrophe caused by NATO's bombings. The same type of analysis sheds light on the Prosecution appeal paragraph 72 as the cited sections do not, in fact, relate to any confirmed crimes being discussed. The only things being discussed: Pre-emptive discipline of forces, avoiding breaches of the cease-fire, and the refugee crisis. Another item that the Prosecution cites is P1468, and in particular, they refer to a meeting - that is at page 37 of the same - and I believe this also demonstrates a misapprehension of the evidence by the Prosecution. Looking specifically at this entry it states in pertinent part that "Mr. Gajo" whom the evidence shows to be David Gajic, the senior state security coordinator for Kosovo, and I would turn to Djakovic, the author of this notebook, testifying as to that fact at T 26370, and this is the entry that the Prosecution in the judgement would like to highlight -- or, excuse me, the Prosecution appeal would like to highlight. "An investigation of six persons was initiated. Three in Malisevo. One of them is giving a statement that he committed murder and rape and three new persons." To properly understand this reference, it must be understood, Your Honours, that Malisevo was KLA-controlled territory in 1998 and, indeed, was declared the capital of KLA-controlled territory. We have that from 3D194 and also the testimony of Bislim Zyrapi of the KLA at 6852 of the transcript. Gajic, as the RDB coordinator was tasked with giving updates on KLA activities as this was part of his mandate. Djakovic testified as to that at transcript page 26430. Hence, Your Honours, in this concrete case that the Prosecution wants to show you that Lukic had knowledge of crimes, the crimes in question from 1998 are actually relating to the KLA and KLA perpetrators that are taken into custody by state security. More striking examples can be drawn from paragraph 72 and the sections of the trial judgement that the Prosecution cites in support of their appeal. I will just touch on a few of them. They cite to paragraph 1082 of book 3. This is the cited testimony of Shaun Byrnes, which actually relates to a fierce battle between Serb forces and the KLA in Kijevo and makes no allegation of crimes. In fact, when questioned about the cause of the burning houses, Byrnes confirmed, we saw the quote yesterday, quote: "I did not see a single PJP officer pull a trigger. I did not see a PJP officer light a house on fire by whatever means." The missing factor that the Prosecution ignores is there was a battle between the KLA and state forces. Book 3, paragraph 1083, cited by the Prosecution, also dealing with Shaun Byrnes. The incidents in question must be taken in context with the other evidence, inclusive of the fact that this incident -- one incidence complained of in this section was a humanitarian operation where buses were organised to take people back to their home villages. Is liability being now asserted because people were forced back to their homes? Concerning Byrnes' testimony, the evidence, indeed the Trial Chamber concluding at book 1, 881, that this area during this time, quote, "was a site of significant combat operations." Thus, Your Honours, terrorists not civilians would have been the target of any actions. And these activities would have to be considered to reach a sound conclusion and a sound judgement. Book 3, paragraph 1120, finding that Lukic was aware that crimes were committed in 1998 by various forces including the PJP and the SAJ which were under his control while deployed in Kosovo. The Prosecution is relying upon this and the underlying evidence for its arguments on appeal. The Chamber referred to the following evidence: The statement of Adamovic, which is 6D1613; the minutes of the MUP staff meeting held on 4 April 1999, which is P1989; and a memorandum by the MUP staff, which is 6D874. Although this finding related to 1998, the Chamber referenced evidence dating from 1999 that does not substantiate the conclusions made at all regards to 1998. The paragraphs cited from Adamovic's statement, and indeed the entire statement, make no mention of crimes by the MUP or Serb forces committed in 1998. Moreover, the Chamber itself at book 3, paragraph 1005, noted as to 6D874 that it was signed by Dragan Ilic rather than by Sreten Lukic. The Chamber's position is untenable and thus the Prosecution's appeal is untenable as it -- as it would require Lukic to have knowledge of items that he did not author and for which it has not been shown that he saw them or had knowledge of the same. There were no orders, no evidence of orders, no indicia of any orders issued by Lukic as to anti-terrorist actions that were adduced at trial. In regards to the memorandum of the MUP staff from 4 April 1999, neither this document nor Lukic's words recorded therein mention or imply any crimes committed by state forces in 1998. The factual backdrop simply does not support the Prosecution's appeal as to foreseeability and therefore that ground should also be repelled. I want to just touch on the aggravating factors that the Prosecution insists on pursuing for which it says a higher sentence is warranted. Both in their brief at paragraph 181 and today in their oral submissions they have claimed that Sreten Lukic was the de facto commander of all the MUP in Kosovo. They consider him a crucial member of the JCE based upon this alleged position as de facto commander, and I understand the seventh ground of appeal as seeking to have this command superior role viewed as an aggravating factor in sentencing. They list four items that they believe show his de facto commander role. The first is Lukic's role in disarming the Albanian population, paragraph 183 of the appeal. I think we have in some detail explained that yesterday and that shows how their argument is misplaced, because Lukic's role was only in working with the international community and with Serbian officials to keep track of voluntary surrenders of weapons in accord with the law and seeking peace. This part of the Prosecution appeal must therefore fail. The second arm that they allege is Lukic's central role in coordinating the exchange of info from the MUP HQ in Belgrade and the MUP in Kosovo. That's paragraph 184 of their appeal. As to this, we have already seen yesterday how the SUPs reported directly to Belgrade and only in parallel to the staff. Further we showed that you the chief of the police administration and commander of all PJP, Obrad Stevanovic, who was a superior -- who was in a superior position in the MUP to Lukic, was on the ground in Kosovo in 1999. Lukic could not supplant Stevanovic and the judgement confirmed that he did not supplant or change the hierarchy of the MUP upon his appointment as head of staff. The third tenet that the Prosecution holds for the de facto commander role of Lukic is his participation in meetings. It's paragraph 182 of their appeal. As to participation in meetings, that too was discussed and I believe rebutted in our submissions yesterday. And I believe the third -- fourth is from paragraph 185 of their appeal, Lukic's direct involvement in planning. We also discussed that yesterday and saw that indeed the Trial Chamber found Lukic did not have a role in preparing the global plan for the suppression of terrorism. Also we would submit how can Lukic be de facto commander of the MUP and deserve a higher sentence if the following is true under the evidence. First, the ability to exercise effective control in the sense of a material power to prevent or punish has been identified by the Appeals Chamber to be a minimum requirement for the purposes of a command superior responsibility. That is paragraph 59 of the Halilovic appeal judgement. The same paragraph concludes as well whereas: "... a police officer may be able to 'prevent and punish' crimes under his jurisdiction ... this would not ... make him a superior ... vis-a-vis any perpetrator within that jurisdiction." Your Honours, it is clear that Lukic didn't have the ability to prevent or punish in the sense of any command superior or leadership role. Thus, it is clear that for the manner of responsibility the Prosecution wishes to assert, it wrongfully assumes that if Lukic reported on crime prevention efforts underway he had control over units through a leadership role. We talked of lack of disciplinary powers already yesterday and today. I would only add that the evidence shows that Lukic could not appoint or replace anyone in the MUP including members of his own staff. 6D1045, 6D1047, 6D1049, 6D1050, 6D1052, and even P1884, P1886, and P1885 demonstrate that proposition. Lukic could not assign or promote anyone within the MUP. 6D1344 and 6D1348 verify that. Further, Lukic could not decide on deployment of PJP units to Kosovo. 6D271, 6D287, 6D291, and 6D1356, among other evidence, demonstrate that. From the foregoing, it is clear under the standard established in Halilovic appeals judgement that irrespective of whether the Brdjanin or Karadzic standard is used, there is no leadership role attributable to Lukic that could form the basis of an aggravation of sentence or ability for -- or liability for sexual assaults. When the totality of the evidence is reviewed under the appropriate standards, we see that Lukic contributed greatly to the investigation of crimes, not to their perpetration. We ask you to repel the Prosecution's appeal. I just want to touch on something that the Prosecution counsel raised today, their claim that persons were expelled from Pristina, Pec, Djakovica, and other towns in Kosovo. Just like yesterday, they would like to ignore the role of the KLA and ignore the role of NATO. And they would like to ignore how these two actors beyond the control of Lukic had an effect on the departure of civilians of all ethnicities in Kosovo. I'd like to now move briefly into private session to discuss some Rule 70 documents and their source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6D1637 is evidence from a Rule 70 provider that Serbs and Albanians in Pristina were facing hardships and choosing to leave that city after and as a result of NATO commencing daytime strikes in Pristina. Was Lukic guilty for NATO's actions? 6D1638 talks of the KLA General Staff reporting that its units are in battle inside the towns of Pec and Djakovica and attempting to take over control of those towns. 6D1636 confirms by the KLA that they have entered the city centre of Pec and were battling for control of Pec. 6D1637 also talks of fierce fighting in Pec between the KLA and state forces as well as the presence of a KLA force and fighting in the Reka and Carragojs region. I ask you, Your Honours, is Lukic supposed to be guilty for the actions of the KLA? These documents and other evidence of record provide alternative reasons why people left their homes and why they fled. Other evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Other evidence that I believe Your Honours need to consider in relation to the Prosecution appeal. We ask you to consider a totality of the evidence and the arguments that we have presented and ask you to repel the Prosecution appeal in its entirety. And I thank you for your time, and I apologise to the translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was wondering if I might have one minute of my time back. I've been searching for a cite and I finally found it. I just want to tell you what it is and where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I remembered this from a long time ago and I was having trouble finding it. It's actually in the first Appeals Chamber decision of this Tribunal, the Erdemovic sentencing appeal. It's on page 14, and what the Appeals Chamber says there is: "The appeal process of the International Tribunal is not designed for the purpose of allowing parties to remedy their own failings or oversights during trial or sentencing." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it's time for a break. We will have 30 minutes' break and we'll resume at quarter past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to inform the Appeals Chamber that my colleague did not feel well and he had to leave the courtroom for the rest of the day so I will be the only counsel representing Mr. Sainovic for the rest of today's hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We all wish him a speedy recovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now the Bench would like to hear the reply from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may it please the Court. To provide you a brief road map of our reply, first I plan on addressing ground 2 of our appeal and, in the context of our reply, address Judge Liu's question. After me, Ms. Jarvis will then proceed on providing a reply regarding responses concerning grounds 3 and 4 of our appeal. And then finally Mr. Kremer will conclude by addressing the responses to ground 1 and 6 of our appeal but also address the question that was asked of Ms. Jarvis concerning the role of the NATO bombings, as well as the number of individuals who fled Kosovo. Your Honours, to begin, first to address Judge Liu's question. The Trial Chamber did not explicitly apply the specific direction test as this was not a requirement before the Perisic appeals judgement as was explained on Wednesday by Mr. Marcussen. Your Honours, I refer you to transcript pages 439 to 461. However, even if you now take the view that specific direction is a requirement, we submit that it was implicitly established by the Trial Chamber in this case. As Mr. Marcussen detailed before, General Lazarevic was a proximate aider and abettor. You can find that at transcript pages 461 to 470. He was on the ground in Kosovo when the crimes were being committed and he was the commander of the forces involved in those crimes. His role, Your Honours, is similar to that of Krstic, Brdjanin, and Simic, all of which the Perisic Appeals Chamber found to be proximate at footnote 100 of paragraph 38. And on Wednesday, we showed you that General Lazarevic specifically contributed to operations which could never be understood as legitimate warfare, in particular, Your Honours, with respect to the Reka Valley operation. Therefore, on the facts of this case, it is implicit that General Lazarevic's actions were specifically directed at the crimes of deportation, forcible transfer, and murder as explained in our submissions on Wednesday and earlier today. Your Honours, as one final note on that question, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that today the Prosecutor for the Special Court of Sierra Leone has recently issued a briefing in that case indicating all of the problems that we discussed concerning the Perisic appeals judgement. Second, Your Honours, General Lazarevic attempts to disclaim his responsibility for these crimes by suggesting that he took steps to combat murders involving the VJ. While we understand that there may be certain circumstances where an accused can absolve themselves of aiding and abetting liability by taking steps to combat crimes, this is not one of those cases. The Prosecution notes that the Trial Chamber considered these arguments at Volume III, paragraph 870, and found that General Lazarevic's responses were, and I quote, "manifestly inadequate in light of the scale of the offences occurring in Kosovo." The Chamber also found that General Lazarevic was aware of these inadequacies, noting at Volume III, paragraph 925, that, and I quote again: "General Lazarevic knew that his failure to take adequate measures to secure the proper investigation of serious crimes committed by the VJ enabled the forces to continue their campaign of terror, violence, and displacement." Your Honours, these are the two issues I wish to discuss concerning ground 2, and unless you have any further questions on this issue, I would now like to turn the podium over to Ms. Jarvis. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll also aim to be quite brief in reply. I have just three points that I wanted to mention in relation to the issue of the sexual assaults as persecution in this case. First of all, both counsel for Sainovic and Lukic emphasise the point that, in their view, the numbers of sexual assaults in this case were quite low and therefore constituted opportunistic assaults that were unconnected with the broader campaign. First of all, as I've mentioned, Your Honours, there's no legal requirement that a crime has to be committed in large numbers in order to be foreseeable for the purposes of JCE III. Nor is there any legal requirement that a crime has to be committed in large numbers to form part of an attack that would constitute a crime against humanity. The case law more generally confirms that even one act could qualify as a crime against humanity or even persecution so long as it's not an isolated act or random. And that's the Kunarac appeals judgement, paragraph 96, and the Blaskic appeal judgement, paragraph 101, just by way of a couple of examples. But as the Defence have asserted that the number of sexual assaults in evidence was low, it's perhaps worth providing a little bit more detail on this point. And to begin I want to correct something that I said in my submissions earlier today where I referred to 11 sexual assault incidents having been charged in the indictment. What I should have said was there are 11 sexual assault incidents found to be proved by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please show down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: I also referred to evidence on the record about an estimated 50 additional sexual assaults. In particular, Your Honours, K58, a witness in relation to Beleg, described how, while K20 and the two other girls were absent from the room, more young women were selected by paramilitaries who came to the rooms about four or five times until approximately 20 young women or girls had been taken, with the last one being returned at around 5.00 a.m. These girls returned disheveled and crying, and K58 overheard one of them telling her mother that she had been raped. That's trial judgement Volume II, paragraph 63. The Trial Chamber found that at least four women were sexually assaulted in Cirez, but there was evidence that around 20 other women were subjected to similar treatment. Trial judgement Volume II, paragraphs 629 to 631. And one of the three victims who the Trial Chamber found had been raped in Pristina stated that around 10 to 15 other Kosovo Albanian women had been taken to the Pristina hospital basement where she was held to be raped. That's Trial judgement Volume II, paragraph 880, and Exhibit P2596. In my submissions earlier I also referred to other reports of rape on the record, and to those I could also add that human rights observers and journalists published reports of rape and sexual assault before, during, and after the 1999 campaign, and I refer to Exhibits P385, P441 and P2228. So for example, after the campaign, Human Rights Watch reported 96 credible reports of sexual assault by Yugoslav soldiers, Serbian police or paramilitaries during the period of the NATO bombing. That's Exhibit P228. So it's not correct, Your Honours, to say, even on the evidentiary record, that the sexual assaults in issue were unusual occurrences. But more fundamentally, even if a crime is opportunistic, it can be foreseeable as confirmed by the Krstic Trial Chamber in relation to the opportunistic rapes in Potocari. My second point, Your Honours, is the reference by my learned colleagues to the fact that the Trial Chamber looked at the Krstic and Kvocka precedence in its judgement and we accept that there was reference to these two cases. But of course, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was applying the wrong legal standard when it carried out its assessment of these two cases. It's for Your Honours to now apply the correct legal standard and draw guidance from the authorities in Krstic and Kvocka to make your own determination. You're not bound by the Trial Chamber's assessment, all the more so given the paucity of reasons given by the Trial Chamber as to how these precedents were to be distinguished from the case at hand. And the third point, Your Honours, is in relation to the arguments we've heard today that the Prosecution is proposing an approach that would result in automatic liability or somehow a kind of strict liability for all sexual violence during armed conflict. We have been at pains, Your Honours, to explain why that's really not the case. We're not talking about the general risk of sexual violence in conflict. We are talking about a situation where there was a common criminal plan which incorporated violence and what is foreseeable in that context. What is missing in the arguments presented to you by my colleagues is the reference, of course, to the fact that their clients signed on to this common criminal purpose. Even so, we're not saying that rape is a foreseeable consequence of every joint criminal enterprise or, indeed, of every ethnic cleansing campaign. Of course, it depends on the methodology employed by the JCE members. Certainly every ethnic cleansing campaign similar to this one which involves unleashing tens of thousands of armed men into villages where they're going to come into one-on-one contact with the targeted population in all of the other conditions that I've mentioned, then yes, it is foreseeable that violations of physical integrity like sexual assault will happen. But of course, we recognise that an ethnic cleansing campaign might be carried out by a different methodology. For example, if shelling was the employed mechanism for trying to terrify people into fleeing, which didn't involve sending troops into villages door-to-door, in that situation, Your Honours, depending on the circumstances, it might well be that a physical violation like sexual assault would not be foreseeable. So we very much recognise that it depends on the particular circumstances but given the nature of this campaign, we say that violations of physical integrity including sexual assault were indeed a foreseeable possibility. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will briefly address some of the responses concerning ground 1 and ground 6. Concerning ground 1, the Prosecution's core case was that Kosovo Albanians were targeted and deported or otherwise forcibly displaced by forces commanded or co-ordinated by the accused. For the reasons that are set out in the Prosecution appeal brief and in our reply brief, the indictment properly pled persecutions by forcible transfer and deportation and the Chamber erred in giving the indictment an overly technical reading resulting in the non-conviction of the persecutions by forcible transfer and deportation. Our position is, and this is set out in paragraphs 8 to 10 of the Prosecution reply brief, there was no waiver. There could be no waiver because the indictment was clear and the Trial Chamber gave it an overly technical reading. I believe that everything that needed to be said is found in the briefs and Your Honours can make your own assessment as to whether or not this position is correct. Concerning ground 6, I have several points. First, counsel for Pavkovic raises his appeal point concerning why his appeal should be mitigated. We deal with this in our response brief at paragraph 149 to 151. His response here is not a response to the Prosecution appeal brief per se. Second, contrary to the submissions made by Pavkovic for each crime identified in Volume II, the Trial Chamber made a specific finding as to which entity, the VJ or the MUP, was involved. Where it could, it also made findings about specific divisions or units involved in the crimes and even differentiated crimes committed by other forces. The crimes were imputed to Pavkovic and other JCE members because the JCE members used the VJ and the MUP forces to carry out the crimes. And I refer you to Volume III, paragraph 783. Third, without responding to our sentencing appeal, counsel for Sainovic went into depth comparing and contrasting Sainovic's responsibility with others who were not charged, or tried in this case, such as Milosevic. While his submissions were passionate calls for the acquittal of his client, they were not a measured response against our submissions concerning Mr. Sainovic's role and responsibility for the crimes and the gravity of the crimes for which he was convicted. Which together, we submit, justified a sentence significantly in excess of 22 years. Fourth, Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Lukic did not respond at all. Mr. Lukic instead took the opportunity to augment his appeal including his sentence appeal, with more references to arguments that he made at trial or included in his appeal brief and were rejected -- arguments which were rejected by the Trial Chamber such as the argument that NATO and the KLA were among the many reasons for the Kosovo Albanian displacement. Issues that the Trial Chamber dealt with squarely and rejected. And this leads me to my next point, counsel for several of the accused argue that the Prosecution should be estopped from arguing anything in excess of 20 years' imprisonment. We comment on this argument in our reply brief. The practice of sentencing in this Tribunal changed before the conclusion of the trial in this case. So there was no sentencing hearing separate from the trial. And at the time the Prosecution was asked to make sentencing submissions, it had no knowledge as to which counts, if any, the accused would be found guilty of. Both the Prosecution and the Defence were required to provide a rough range of possible sentences depending on whether the accused were convicted of one or more crimes and depending on the convicted mode of liability. Contrary to what is being asserted by the accused, the Prosecution did not simply ask for sentences of 20 years at trial. It requested 20 years to life depending on which specific mode of liability and which crimes the accused are found guilty. I refer you to our final trial brief at paragraph 1100 and the trial transcript at page 26947. 20 years was our minimum suggested sentence, assuming the accused were found guilty of only one of the crimes and the lowest mode of liability. The Defence would have you believe that when the Prosecution gives a sentencing range, it should be limited to arguing that on appeal, regardless of the outcome of the trial and regardless of the breadth or narrowness of the convictions. We respectfully disagree. The Chamber in this case went beyond convicting the accused to just one of the crimes under the lowest mode of liability. All four accused were convicted of committing or aiding and abetting the forcible displacement of hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians. The JCE members were convicted of other crimes flowing from their criminal campaign. The accused, in our submission, deserve the severest punishment this Tribunal -- or this Chamber believes is appropriate. In our submission, the Trial Chamber had the responsibility to send a clear message to those who perpetrate crimes on this scale that they will receive the most severe sentences for their crimes. In this -- in not doing this, we submit, the Trial Chamber erred, and we ask you to correct this error and significantly increase the sentences for all four accused. Let me now turn to Judge Tuzmukhamedov's question that was asked this morning of Ms. Jarvis, and the question I understand, just so that we can frame the question I'm answering and if it is -- it requires more amplification I'd welcome it. Where the Trial Chamber beyond reasonable doubt based on evidence other that reports of the MUP made a conclusion that the displacement of upwards of 700.000 could be attributed to the common plan of the members of the joint criminal enterprise. And I'll try to answer the question as we understand it in detail. In paragraph 45 of Volume III, the Chamber found that although the NATO bombing and the KLA activities were a factor in the complicated situation on the ground in 1999, these were not the cause of over 700.000 people moving en masse both within Kosovo and then across the border. In reaching this conclusion, the Trial Chamber took into account the following seven factors. First, the direct and consistent testimony of the Kosovo Albanian witnesses and victims who testified at trial about their own expulsions and that of many others from Kosovo and who said that they left Kosovo because of the actions of the FRY and Serb forces, not the NATO bombing. And that's found at Volume II, paragraphs 33, 69, 163, 279, 285, 887, 915, 942, and 973. In assessing their testimony, the Chamber considered the fact that these witnesses came from a broad section or cross-section of that community generally with no connection to one another beyond their victimisation and found that it was inconceivable that they could or would all have concocted such detail and consistent accounts of the events that they experienced and witnessed. That's Volume II, paragraph 1175. Second, the Chamber took into account the testimony of former MUP and VJ personnel who directly participated in expelling of the Kosovo Albanian civilians from their homes in different municipalities. And I refer the Chamber to Volume II, paragraphs 1172 to 1174; Volume III, paragraph 43. And to also look at Volume II, paragraph 74, 145, 152 to 155, 163, 228 to 232, 235 to 237, 398 to 401, 469 to 470, 498 to 507, 831, 997 to 999, and 1067. Third, the testimony of internationals who were on the ground and confirmed the consistent account of the victims. I refer you to Volume II, paragraph 836 in particular, but also Volume II, paragraphs 848 to 850, 858; Volume II, footnote 2820, in particular Knut Vollebaek, transcript 9522 to 9524, testifying on 31 January 2007. They also took into account data from the UNHCR on the numbers of refugees crossing into Macedonia, Albania and Montenegro. I refer you to footnote -- to Volume II, footnote 2820; Exhibit P2438, redacted statement of Neill Wright of the UNHCR; P738, the UNHCR estimates of displacement and return. Fifth, the fact that NATO bombs struck targets across the FRY with Belgrade suffering the most destruction and yet people did not leave Belgrade and other parts of the FRY in the massive numbers which fled Kosovo. It's a finding at Volume II, paragraph 1177. Sixth, the fact that in the summer of 1998, despite the ongoing conflict between the VJ and the MUP and the KLA, there was no massive flood of people across the borders. Volume 1, paragraph 1177. And finally, the MUP's own reports of the numbers of people crossing the border into Albania, Macedonia, and Montenegro. Volume I, paragraph 1150. It was based on this wide range of mutually corroborating factors, based on direct evidence and circumstantial evidence from witnesses who testified about their own experiences, their own observation, and documented numbers by not only the MUP but other organisations that the Chamber reasonably concluded that, first, the reason for the departure of the Kosovo Albanian civilians was the violence directed against them by forces under the control of the FRY and Serbian authorities, not the NATO bombing. And I refer you again to Volume II, paragraph 1178, which has been referred to during the Prosecution submissions. And this forcible displacement could only be attributed to the common plan of the members of the JCE. And that's found at Volume III, paragraphs 95 to 96. The Trial Chamber's conclusion as to the reason and numbers of people forcibly displaced by the action of the JCE members to implement their common plan was a reasonable one and is entitled to considerable deference. As an Appeals Chamber, you must ask yourselves if this conclusion was one no reasonable Trial Chamber could make, and because this is not a de novo review, it is our submission that the Trial Chamber's conclusion was in fact reasonable. And I hope I've answered your question in full.

utterances.text: Your Honour, at the beginning of the -- what was a reply of the Prosecution, they injected some completely new matter into this case, telling you what the Prosecutor for the STL said about the Perisic case. And if you're willing to treat that at about the same level you'd treat it from a chief Defence counsel in an international court, then I don't have any problem with it, but I don't think it has any impact at all.
