I don't know where the Prosecutor found it. But in any event, if they could provide it to us and we could be allowed to respond to it, that would be okay, or I think it would be much easier to just say it has no meaning and we just let it go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I would like to thank you very much for your submission, but, however, this is a legal document of other Tribunals which has no binding force upon this Tribunal. And according to the Scheduling Order of this hearing, I would like to invite the defendants to make their personal statement if they wish to do so. Yes, Mr. Sainovic, you have the floor. You have ten minutes. THE APPELLANT SAINOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I was a state official. I was elected into the federal parliament back in 1986, and from the parliament into a number of governments in the 1990s. I was still in my term of office as a federal deputy when I came before this Tribunal in 2002. Such an election, of course, implies assuming proportional responsibility for the state of a country. A state official represents the state in good times and bad. In good times there are many of those who take credit for it. In bad times, a state official does not have the right to shy from responsibility and it is in that sense that I stand before you. There were times earlier on when the federal government would send me to Vienna and to Kuwait and those were nice times. When the crisis broke out, it sent me to Kosovo twice before and near the end of the war and that's how I happened to be there. The war in 1999 was exceptionally complex. On the ground there was a clash between the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia and the KLA which used civilians as its base when on offensive activities and would merge with civilians in defensive activities. From the air there was a large scale combat activity of the greatest power in the world whose technical superiority often kept it out of reach or was often unavailable and out of reach of the Army of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This gave an unparalleled dynamic and intensity of the conflict. I would truly not want to wish upon anyone who would wish to compare it to 1998 to be in a position to experience the difference in person. The activity of all these forces at the same time led to appalling civilian casualties in Kosovo and across Yugoslavia. The enormous human suffering is felt to this day. I myself will suffer for it as long as I live. Only the four of us from one side of the conflict are at trial here. Am I aware that as a participant in the events preceding the war and during the war I am answerable for the consequences of my actions? I am aware of it. Why did I plead not guilty here? Precisely for that. That was how I pled in respect of the indictment which substantially distorted the picture of the situation in my country and my role in it, and this is what I have been fighting against in these proceedings for more than ten years now. Was there a meaning to this struggle? I believe that there was, and I will give you an example. Over the past several days, all the parties to the proceedings challenged specific portions of the trial judgement. However, nobody challenged the part where it was found that my country entered into peace negotiations in good faith and that it wasn't to blame for the failed negotiations at Rambouillet as the indictment alleged. In Volume I, paragraphs 407 and 410. I participated in these negotiations with a deep conviction that peace was possible, both for me and my country. This finding constitutes a significant outcome even if it may have cost me ten years. Unfortunately, the Trial Chamber convicted me even for that which I did not participate in and for the position that I did not hold in the relevant period. Although its findings were different from the allegations in the indictment, nevertheless, they were in essence far from the situation as it was in reality. This is the subject matter of my appeal which is before you, Your Honours. I fully stand by everything that my Defence counsel stated here, and I have nothing to add to that. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Pavkovic. You also have ten minutes. THE APPELLANT PAVKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Lieutenant-General of the VJ, retired, Nebojsa Pavkovic, a participant in the events of the 1998 and 1999. I am a professional soldier who has completed all the various military schools with highest credit and I have carried out various duties from the lowest to the highest level and held various positions. I built my career long before I met Mr. Milosevic, which was in late May 1998. I spent six years at Kosovo. I was an operational at the corps and then a Chief of Staff of the corps and then the commander of the corps. The appointment of a commander of a corps is not carried out the way the Prosecutor described it. Out of 760 cadets who graduated from the academy, only 20 per cent are generals. Five were corps commanders, one was army commander, and one was Chief of the General Staff. In 1998, I held the duty of the corps commander and received orders solely from the army commander, General Samardzic. The Chief of the General Staff, Perisic, never issued me with a single order. Milosevic, the president, never issued me with a single order. Mr. Sainovic, for whom I have respect, never issued me an order and, with all due respect, I would never accept an order from Mr. Sainovic who has no military training. And to tell you the truth, if somebody asked me why I am [as interpreted] here, I wouldn't be able to give you an answer. Your Honours, I found it hard that I should be accused as a Serbian general who waged a war against my own people, because the Albanians are my own people. I know them well and I have many friends among them. That's why I would like to draw your attention to several factors which led to the creation of the climate as described in the indictment. This was primarily an unlawful terrorist organisation which tried to achieve its goals through terrorist actions and it was declared a terrorist organisation in March of 1998. Furthermore, the lawful forces of a sovereign independent state, a member of the United Nations, its army and the MUP were trying to combat terrorism in an area. You have to understand the fact that there were 1.403 settlements in Kosovo of which 1.050 were Albanian, 150 were Serbian, and the rest were mixed. Every Albanian village had armed men. This was a tradition. There were -- there was armed guard. There were patrols, and there were more than 100.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "10.000"] pieces of weaponry in the hands of the Albanians. It is important for me to say that the climate of terror in Kosovo was not produced by the law enforcement agencies of the Republic of Yugoslavia. Rather, it was the terrorists of the national army of Kosovo. 80 per cent of the territory of Kosovo was blocked in 1998, 90 per cent of roads were blocked and, later on, as the roads leading to the frontier were blocked as well, the Yugoslav state organs decided that terrorism in Kosovo be combatted with the use of the VJ and MUP. We embarked on this operation and completed it in October 1998. There were no crimes committed. There were crimes committed in Rznici, Jablanicko Lake, et cetera, committed by the Albanians. All the civilians [Realtime transcript read in error "sips"] who were displaced returned to their homes. After the arrival of the OSCE mission, the army withdrew into the barracks, the MUP left Kosovo and Metohija, the KLA took all the positions. I would like to explain to you why the civilians had moved in the first place. I don't have much time but I may be able to explain. As the Prosecutor highlighted, the population moved from 30 municipalities which are in the border area of Kosovo and Metohija. In operative and tactical terms they are on the front line of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps. Those were the positions that were taken by the units of the Army of Yugoslavia pursuant to an order from the Grom 3 directive. It was ordered that those positions be taken. At the moment when we started moving, we were attacked by the KLA and what happened was serious conflicts. Let me just emphasise that in the course of 1998, 1.845 terrorist attacks were carried out in Kosovo. A total of 368 people were killed, out of which 208 civilians, 757 -- or, rather, 758 civilians were killed, 158 were kidnapped. And you can tell from all that who was it who spread the climate of terror. The Army of Yugoslavia, the Pristina Corps namely, had about 11.000 men. Of that the combat segment of the Pristina Corps represented 5.001 men. Everybody else was engaged on the border, deployed on the security detail around various military facilities and so on and so forth. I don't want to talk about NATO. NATO is a military organisation, the most powerful organisation that attacked my country, my small army, and we defended ourselves as best as we could. The biggest problem for us were terrorists, i.e., the KLA. I can tell you that the KLA, on the 1st of January until the 23rd of March, carried out 632 attacks. 101 against the army, 298 against the MUP, and 233 against the civilians. Every day 6 to 8 attacks on average. This is an analysis, and all the evidence may be found among the tens of thousands of exhibits that we have seen here and that we have submitted. When it comes to civilians, three to four civilians were killed every day. And they were killed by terrorists. When it comes the deportation of civilians, as the Prosecutor calls that, even up to 1998, from 1981, whenever conflicts happened in Kosovo, whenever there was disorder, civilians fled the territory of Kosovo. It happened all the time. In 1998 it didn't happen, but they again started leaving Kosovo in 1999 from those 13 municipalities that were along the borders. There are 29 municipalities in Kosovo. We heard arguments why people did not leave the remaining 16 municipalities, why there were not conflicts there because there were no terrorists there. There was no need for exodus from those municipalities. We had the fiercest battles with terrorists during the aggression, and with this regard, I would like to point out that the NATO campaign contributed largely to the movement of civilians. During the 78 days of the aggression, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia suffered 3.380 air-strikes. In Kosovo, 1.574 air-strikes, which accounted for over 50 per cent of the total number of air-strikes. Cities in Kosovo that suffered air-strikes, Pristina 406, Prizren 334, Urosevac 240, Pec 108, Kosovska Mitrovica 116 times. 752 settled areas in Kosovo suffered air-strikes, some of them 5 to 8 times. The units of the 3rd Army suffered 4.662 projectiles thrown at them. That means that --

Mr. Lazarevic, may I invite you to make a personal statement, if you wish, for ten minutes. THE APPELLANT LAZAREVIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, honourable members of the Appeals Chamber, I would like to thank you for giving me the opportunity to address you. I would like to draw your attention briefly to some aspects of the factual context from the military doctrine aspect. Nothing has been said about that here these days. I would like to point out that 19 members of NATO, in the spring of 1999, carried out a classical foreign aggression against Yugoslavia. They engaged the first and the fifth echelons of the forces of the separatist terrorist armed rebellion. It all resulted in a practical simulation of the exodus of Albanian civilians. In terms of the forces that were engaged, the types and the power and the quantity of lethal weapons which were used in Kosovo and Metohija, they were tantamount to an equivalent of 8 to 10 nuclear bombs that thrown on Hiroshima, and especially in terms of its brutality and its targets, in view of the international and [indiscernible] aggression was one of the most asymmetrical wars ever conducted in the world. And while that war for some who provoked it was a modern war, for others it was a campaign. I don't understand the word "campaign." For the leadership of the terrorists it was a guerrilla total war, that's what they call it. And for military and geopolitical analysts in the world, it was also a nuclear war because 31.000 nuclear radioactive projectiles were deployed in as many as 102 locations. Over the next 4.5 billion years they will continue bringing death and misfortune to Serbia. At the same time, to date, this has been the only near neocortical war ever conducted in the history of the world. NATO achieved its goals on the 24th of March, 1999, and it did not pay much attention to its targets. The complete border area was carpeted by aerial bombs. Everything that looked like a possible military threat, including even wooden pillars, everything was their target. Densely populated urban neighbourhoods were targeted every day, several hundred times in one city. Easily discernible commercial and production facilities were especially interesting, as well as the long columns of red Albanian tractors belonging to Albanian civilians which were on their way back to their homes. Even the famous Charlie, the famous aircraft pilot, could distinguish them from Serbian tanks. NATO commanders ordered the massacre of those civilians and the whole world is aware of that. In the territory of the region alone, NATO carried out 2.000 air-strikes or 30 air-strikes every day. There were several hundreds of rocket strikes, and in all of those attacks, civilian targets accounted for 36 to 38 per cent of all the targets. Unfortunately, Your Honours, these are irrefutable, horrendous, terrible facts describing NATO aggressors' activities in the area and its contribution to the misfortune of all those who happened to found themselves there at the time. Truth be told, or, rather, it is true that in Kosovo and Metohija alone, NATO killed as many as 500 civilians and destroyed over 700 various facilities. These facts cannot be masked by any conflation, by exhibitions, or by the abolition of those who caused all that misfortune. In the territory of the region during the war, death came from high altitudes, from distances over 2.500 kilometres, across -- from across the border facing Albania on a front line stretching for several dozens of kilometres, from a hundred of Albanian villages which had been transformed into terrorist strongholds or paramilitary bases. According to the principle of two villages of which one was a terrorist stronghold and the other served for the removal of civilians into them. The tactic of Mao Tse-tung of a thousand fires was applied which means from all sides, from all places at any time. In the conditions of such a war inferno and war chaos, the population sought salvation in flight, movement, transfer, in seeking shelter, like anywhere elsewhere where there's death and where is fire. Their roads led to Albania, Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Turkey, Croatia, to far away countries in the West, as far as possible away from death. The UNHCR data say that 54 per cent of the Serbian and non-Albanian population of the region and 45 per cent of the Albanian population sought refuge outside of the territory of the region during the war. In Kosovo and Metohija, members of the Pristina Corps did not have a place to flee from death. They suffered as much as 95 per cent of the losses of the total losses of the Army of Yugoslavia, and the same destiny was shared by several hundred thousand of Albanian civilians who believed that they would survive with the help of the Pristina Corps. And this is still the talk of the day among Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija. Therefore at the beginning of spring over 14 years ago, at the focal point of the strategic defence in the war inferno, the Pristina Corps found itself in a strategic trap faced with a mission impossible. In such conditions which would have been difficult to tackle by any military, the corps -- the corps employed a tactic that immediately after the war NATO named the 4M tactic - masking, manoeuvre, mobility, morale. When translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I believe that your time is up. So you may have one more minute to finish your statement. THE APPELLANT LAZAREVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Judges of the Appeals Chamber, at ten Status Conferences I advised the President, during 122 minutes in total, with the status of my health. In June last year, the last team of medical consultants concluded that I was a patient whose health is seriously undermined, requiring urgent measures to bring his health up to a tolerable level and I would say at least up to the level of a detainee. In the past year there have been no such measures. God help me, but I also hope the Registry will not forget me either, or the Trial -- or the Appeals Chamber, as far as my health is concerned. Your Honours, thank you for your attention. Thank you for your patience and your understanding, I hope. Merci beaucoup, xiexie, spasiba, grazie, tesekkur ederim. [Interpretation] My gratitude is sincere, and I hope you will excuse me for my bad pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Lukic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interruption, Your Honour. With your leave, just one correction in transcript. Page 110, line 22, I think that the words "under the order of KLA" missing in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you also have ten minutes to make a personal statement. You also have ten minutes to make your personal statement. THE APPELLANT LUKIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I'm truly sorry and I truly regret all the casualties, especially the civilian ones, and the suffering of the citizens caused by the unfortunate war in Kosovo. I want to tell you that I did not go to Kosovo of my own volition, but following orders and the law. I went there neither willingly nor voluntarily. My assignment to Kosovo was the result of a regular rotation of the head of staff that was done annually for a number of years before that. The duties I was sent to perform were the police duties envisaged by the constitution and the law. The safety of both the Serbs and the Albanians was extremely jeopardised by the criminal activities of the terrorist organisation that called itself the KLA. The authority of the staff and me as its head was rather limited. The staff was not a command body and I was not a commander, neither de jure nor de facto. Thus, for example, I was not authorised to decide on or institute any disciplinary, misdemeanour or criminal proceedings against police officers who violated the law. I was not in a position to suspend or dismiss any senior police officer. You will agree without those powers there can be no command function. That I was not a commander is also confirmed by the following fact: On the eve of the bombing, Minister Stojilkovic informed me that, as agreed with President Milosevic, he had sent his assistant, Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic to Kosovo with the task of commanding and controlling all the Ministry of Interior forces for the duration of the state of war. The evidence confirms that this was indeed case. In addition to being an assistant minister and the chief of police administration, General Obrad Stevanovic was also de jure and de facto the commander of all the PJP units of the Serbian MUP. Besides the three functions he discharged, Obrad Stevanovic was also known to be fully trusted by Stojilkovic and Milosevic alike. When the bombing started, the security situation became dramatic. All those who found themselves in Kosovo were in danger, especially civilians. Despite my limited powers and authority, I demanded that the civilian population be additionally protected and that all perpetrators of crimes be arrested. During the 78 days of the bombing and constant terrorist attacks, the police identified and filed criminal reports against at least 785 perpetrators. 443 of whom were arrested immediately. Over 95 per cent of them were Serbs, including 46 policemen and 97 soldiers. Almost all of the crimes concerned were committed against the Kosovo Albanians. My commitment and my insistence on arresting anyone who committed crimes was met with disapproval by some of the Serbian political leaders in Kosovo. The most prominent among them intended even to have me liquidated because of the arrests of police officers who had killed Albanian civilians. I faced no less serious threats again in 2001, when I initiated the investigation of the mass graves and the crimes against Albanians. Everything I did in my entire professional career was for protecting citizens. I never discriminated against people on ethnic or any other grounds. I was brought up in this spirit and trained to act in this manner since I was 15. During my tenure in Kosovo, I did not personally commit any crime, nor did I order, plan, instigate, aid, conceal or otherwise participate in any crime. All my actions, every word I said, and every letter I wrote were aimed at preventing crimes. Therefore, I wish to emphasise once again that I am not guilty of any crimes that I have been convicted of. And I did not know of any of these crimes at the time. I found out about the joint criminal enterprise from the indictment. I was never aware of any plan, intent or objective to have the Kosovo Albanians expelled. No one ever requested or suggested to me to do anything of that sort, and if they had, I most certainly would not have participated in it. I cannot accept the finding in the judgement that I was a member of a joint criminal enterprise headed by Milosevic. It was only after being sent to Kosovo in mid-1998, that I was personally introduced to Milosevic, Milutinovic, Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lazarevic. I was never a favourite or a confidante of Milosevic or of Minister Stojilkovic or of his assistants Djordjevic and Stevanovic. Quite the contrary, all I ever experienced from them was humiliation and degradation. This fact was common knowledge Serbia. Hence the decision of the government that was formed after the fall of Milosevic to have me promoted and appoint me as chief of police of Serbia. Moreover, foreign intelligence agencies that were involved in the background checks before my appointment had no objections as to my conduct in Kosovo. Your Honours, these are some of the facts. I hope you will take into account in your deliberations regarding the appeal brief and our oral submissions. I hope that your decision will remedy the injustice done to me by the trial judgement. Thank you very much for allowing me to address you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Any other corrections?
